userStories.title: Edge builds ship with release="dev" — every prod edge error is unattributable to a commit (frontend is correct)
userStories.description: As GradeThread, we want to know which build produced a production error. The frontend does: https://gradethread.com serves a bundle tagged release:"c9631342084bfd9e96883321a07a390d3be1e814", a real commit SHA, so Cloudflare Pages is wiring VITE_RELEASE_SHA correctly. The EDGE does not: GET https://functions.gradethread.com/health returns {"env":"production","release":"dev"}, measured 2026-07-18. Root cause is exact — services/edge-functions/Dockerfile:12 declares ARG GIT_SHA=dev and line 13 sets ENV RELEASE_SHA=${GIT_SHA}; its own comment (lines 9-11) says the builder must pass GIT_SHA=$SOURCE_COMMIT, and the Coolify build is not doing so, so the literal default ships. lib/observability.ts:52 releaseSha() therefore returns "dev" and tags every Sentry event, structured log and trace with it. This is an ASYMMETRY between the two halves of the system, and the half that is blind is the one handling grading, payments, eBay writes and webhooks.
acceptanceCriteria: The Coolify build passes the commit into the image (GIT_SHA build arg = $SOURCE_COMMIT or the platform equivalent), so RELEASE_SHA is a real SHA in production.
GET /health on production returns a release that matches the deployed commit — verify by measuring the endpoint after a deploy, not by reading the config.
Sentry edge events carry that release, so an error can be attributed to a deploy and "did the fix ship?" is answerable. Confirm a real event is tagged.

A guard so this cannot silently regress: the edge should REFUSE to report healthy-and-production while release is the literal default "dev"/"unknown" — or at minimum surface it as a degraded feature in /health/ready features{} alongside the existing observability entry, which currently reports "ok" while the release is meaningless.
Document the build-arg requirement in COOLIFY.md next to the other deploy settings, since the Dockerfile comment alone did not survive contact with the actual deploy.
userStories.notes: [P2][Ops/Observability][Measured] Found 2026-07-18 during the cross-platform production-readiness deep dive, by querying prod rather than reading config. EVIDENCE, all live: /health -> {"status":"ok","service":"gradethread-edge-functions","env":"production","release":"dev","errorTracking":"enabled"}; the frontend bundle /assets/index-CIbHzx5V.js contains release:"c9631342084bfd9e96883321a07a390d3be1e814" (which is also proof Pages auto-deployed that commit). WHY IT MATTERS MORE THAN A COSMETIC TAG: with every edge event tagged "dev" you cannot (a) attribute a production error to a build, (b) tell whether a deployed fix actually shipped, (c) see a regression appear at a release boundary, or (d) make a rollback decision on evidence — and ROLLBACK.md assumes you can identify the bad build. Note errorTracking reports "enabled" and /health/ready features.observability reports "ok", so the health surface actively says observability is fine while the release dimension of it is inert; that is why AC4 asks for a guard rather than just a config fix. The fix itself is small (one build arg); the reason it survived this long is that nothing measured it. | 2026-07-19 AC1/AC4/AC5 DONE; AC2/AC3 need a deploy to confirm. THE ROOT CAUSE WAS A MISSING BUILD ARG, and the fix is DECLARATIVE rather than another instruction: docker-compose.coolify.yml now carries build.args GIT_SHA: dev. That placement is the whole point — the Dockerfile has carried a comment telling the builder to pass GIT_SHA since it was written, and per this story's own evidence that comment did not survive contact with the actual deploy. A build arg in compose is APPLIED BY THE PLATFORM instead of remembered by a person, so documenting it harder would have reproduced the same failure. The :-dev fallback keeps a plain local docker compose build working. AC4 DONE and it is the anti-regression half: the observability feature group now requires SENTRY_DSN *and* a real RELEASE_SHA, so /health/ready reports observability DEGRADED while the release is a placeholder — previously it reported 'ok' in the exact prod state this story measured (errorTracking enabled, release 'dev'), which is the false confidence that let it sit unnoticed. isRealReleaseSha is deliberately permissive on FORM: it rejects the placeholder set (dev/unknown/local/none/latest/empty) but accepts short SHAs and tags, because the measured failure was the literal ARG default surviving the build, not a malformed SHA — requiring 40 hex chars would break tag-based deploys for no benefit. 4 tests, including the exact prod state as a case. AC5 DONE in COOLIFY.md with a MEASURE-DO-NOT-READ verification step (curl /health | jq .release), plus the warning that deploying from docker-compose.yml rather than the .coolify.yml variant needs the same args block. ⚠ REMAINING AND GENUINELY UNVERIFIABLE FROM HERE: AC2 (measure /health after a deploy) and AC3 (confirm a real Sentry event carries the release). Both require the deploy to actually happen. What HAS changed is that a regression now announces itself on /health/ready instead of waiting for someone to think to curl. [2026-07-19 AC4+AC5 DONE, AC1-AC3 NEED THE COOLIFY BUILD + A PROD MEASUREMENT] AC4: /health/ready now carries features.release, degraded whenever the release is unattributable (dev / unknown / empty / whitespace, case-insensitive). Deliberately a SEPARATE key from features.observability: that group reports ok whenever a Sentry DSN is present, which stays true and stays misleading while every event it ships is tagged dev. Also deliberately does NOT flip the service to not_ready — the AC allowed either, and refusing readiness on an untagged build would pull grading, payments and webhooks out of rotation to protect observability. health.ts already argues this exact principle for the schema probe (a probe that can fail a container over a diagnostic is a worse bug than the blind spot it fixes). A test asserts ready stays true. releaseReadiness() is pure; 5 new tests. AC5 FINDING: COOLIFY.md already had a US-2001 build-args section from an earlier pass, and it CLAIMED /health/ready reports features.observability as degraded on a placeholder release. That was FALSE — nothing implemented it. The documentation described a guard that did not exist, which is a plausible reason nobody built one; same defect class as US-2035 (comment asserting a property the code lacks) and US-2123 (copy advertising an ungranted entitlement). Doc now names the real key, shows the curl, and records the correction rather than quietly overwriting it. STILL OPEN (all need the deploy, not code): AC1 the Coolify build must actually pass GIT_SHA=$SOURCE_COMMIT — docker-compose.coolify.yml declares it but prod measured release=dev on 2026-07-18, so either the deploy uses docker-compose.yml or the Build Args field is unset. AC2 verify by curling /health after a deploy. AC3 confirm a real Sentry event carries the SHA. The new features.release entry makes AC2 checkable without remembering the curl.

userStories.title: GDPR erasure misses an entire class of email-keyed PII, including full rendered email bodies
userStories.description: As a data subject, when I delete my account I want my personal data actually erased. Both the erasure endpoint (routes/account.ts:310-496) and the RPC (00043_delete_account_rpc.sql:33-36) rely EXCLUSIVELY on the ON DELETE CASCADE chain rooted at auth.users, which reaches only tables with an FK to users. These tables hold real PII keyed by EMAIL and are untouched: email_deliveries (recipient, subject, and html — the full rendered body of every critical email, 00095:9-13), email_consent_audit (email, ip, 00296:36), email_subscribers, marketing_send_log, waitlist_entries, newsletter_issue_recipients (no FK at all), email_journey_step_sends, guarantee_claims (third-party buyer PII). The ON DELETE SET NULL cases are sharpest: they sever the link while PRESERVING the email address — the exact identifier a subject would cite in an erasure complaint. account.ts:306-307 asserts the cascade 'wipes every public table keyed to it', which is true and precisely the wrong invariant, because these are keyed to an email.
acceptanceCriteria: Add an explicit email-keyed purge before auth.admin.deleteUser: delete from email_deliveries / marketing_send_log / email_journey_step_sends / newsletter_issue_recipients by the user email; anonymize email_consent_audit / waitlist_entries / email_subscribers.
email_suppressions is a DELIBERATE exception — a suppression list must survive erasure or the user starts receiving mail again. Hash the address there rather than deleting it, and document why.
Add a test asserting that after deletion NO row in any table matches the deleted address. That assertion is the only durable guard, since the bug class is 'a new table keyed by email'.
Re-word the comment at account.ts:306-307 so the next reader is not reassured by an invariant that does not cover email-keyed tables.
userStories.notes: [P1][Compliance/GDPR] Found 2026-07-18 by the data-integrity deep dive. Severity comes precisely from the endpoint SUCCEEDING: it returns {deleted:true} and sends a confirmation email while the address and the full HTML of every payment-failed and grade-ready message remain queryable forever. The surrounding compliance work is genuinely good — account.ts export, a deletion log that does not block erasure on logging failure (:439-442), data-retention keeping the non-PII grade while purging PII — which is what makes this gap easy to miss: everything around it is correct. | 2026-07-18 FIXED (agent loop). AC1 DONE: account.ts step 3c purges email-keyed PII BEFORE auth.admin.deleteUser (ordering is load-bearing — after the cascade users.email is gone and there is nothing left to key the purge on). ⚠ I CORRECTED THE STORY'S OWN PRESCRIPTION while implementing it: the AC said to ANONYMIZE waitlist_entries and email_subscribers, but both declare email as NOT NULL (and UNIQUE), so nulling would simply fail and leave the PII sitting there — an 'anonymize' that silently no-ops is worse than no attempt, because the code reads as handled. Those two are hard-DELETEd instead (a deleted account has no waitlist position to hold and no subscription to keep; unsubscribe protection does NOT depend on them — that is email_suppressions). Hard-delete: email_deliveries (the one carrying full rendered html bodies), marketing_send_log, email_journey_step_sends, newsletter_issue_recipients, waitlist_entries, email_subscribers. Anonymize: email_consent_audit (email + ip nulled) because both columns ARE nullable and the row proves WHEN a consent action happened — a record that outlives the subject once identifiers are gone. Every column name was VERIFIED against the migrations rather than assumed; these tables disagree on whether the column is `recipient` or `email`, and a wrong name would look exactly like a successful purge (we log the 42703 and continue). AC2 DONE: email_suppressions deliberately preserved + a test that fails if anyone starts deleting it, because forgetting a bounced/complained address makes it start receiving mail again — harming the very person erasure protects. AC4 DONE: the endpoint header comment claimed the cascade 'wipes every public table keyed to it', which was reassuring in exactly the wrong way; it now states that the cascade covers user_id-keyed tables ONLY and points at step 3c. NEW TEST account-email-purge_test.ts (4 cases). The durable one is an INVENTORY GUARD that rediscovers candidates from the migration corpus — any table declaring an email/recipient/claimant_email text column, not cascade-deleted from users, and not handled by the route, fails the build with an explicit EXEMPT escape hatch. userStories.title: The data-retention PII sweep cannot advance past its first batch — GDPR retention silently unenforced
userStories.description: As GradeThread, we want expired submission images actually purged. lib/data-retention.ts:36-50 selects submissions past the cutoff with NO filter for whether images remain and NO ORDER BY, despite the comment claiming 'still have images to purge'. It takes 200 arbitrary expired submissions, looks up their images (:53-56), and returns early when there are none (:63-65). So after the first run purges those 200, every subsequent nightly run re-selects the same already-purged rows, finds zero images, and returns {objects_deleted: 0} — newer expired submissions are NEVER reached. The cron stays perpetually green while enforcement stopped at run two.
acceptanceCriteria: Filter to submissions that still HAVE images and order deterministically, e.g. .select('id, submission_images!inner(id)').lt('created_at', cutoff).order('created_at', {ascending:true}).limit(BATCH_LIMIT).
Add a regression test asserting a SECOND sweep over a fresh dataset still returns objects_deleted > 0 — the single assertion that distinguishes this bug from correct behaviour.
Backfill: quantify how much past-retention imagery accumulated while the sweep was stalled, and drain it.
Emit an ops event when a sweep finds nothing across N consecutive runs while past-cutoff rows exist.
userStories.notes: [P1][Compliance/GDPR] Found 2026-07-18 by the data-integrity deep dive. Compounds two other findings: the purged originals are EXIF/GPS-bearing (account.ts:377-379), and enforcement also depends on a hand-registered Coolify cron that nothing monitors (see the cron-stall story). A perpetually-green cron doing nothing is the pattern this whole session keeps finding — a check that reports success is indistinguishable from one that works, unless something asserts the work happened. | 2026-07-18 FIXED (agent loop). The scan now drives off submission_images joined to submissions!inner(created_at), filtered on submissions.created_at < cutoff, ordered created_at ASC, limited to BATCH_LIMIT. That choice is deliberate and structural rather than cosmetic: the sweep can no longer stall BY CONSTRUCTION, because the query only ever returns rows that still exist and deleting them is precisely what this function does, so every run strictly advances. (The alternative — keeping the submissions-first scan but adding an images-exist filter — would have worked too, but it leaves the two-step shape that made the stall possible in the first place.) ORDER BY added so 'the next 200' is a well-defined set instead of Postgres row order. submissions_processed is now the distinct submission count within the batch, so the reported metric keeps its meaning. NEW TEST src/tests/data-retention_test.ts (3 cases) — and I want to be honest about what it is: a STRUCTURAL guard, not a behavioural one. purgeExpiredGradingPii talks to the service-role client with no injection seam, so two sweeps over a fixture would need a live DB (that belongs in the db lane). But the defect IS a property of query shape, so shape is the right thing to pin. NEGATIVE-VERIFIED: I checked out the original buggy version and all three assertions failed, then restored the fix and all three passed — the guard demonstrably catches the real historical bug rather than merely describing it. STILL OPEN: AC3 (quantify + drain the backlog of past-retention imagery that accumulated while the sweep was stalled — needs prod DB access) and AC4 (ops event when a sweep repeatedly finds nothing while past-cutoff rows exist). | 2026-07-19 AC4 DONE. The sweep now NOTICES when it stops advancing. AC1 and AC2 shipped previously (query shape fixed, structural guard added and negative-verified against the original buggy version); this is the RUNTIME counterpart, and the distinction is the point: the shape guard proves the code is right TODAY, while this proves the BEHAVIOUR is right in production — which is the thing that actually failed. A stall can return in a form no source assertion would catch: a bad cutoff, an RLS change, a storage outage, a permissions regression. THE SIGNAL IS DELIBERATELY A CONJUNCTION — zero objects deleted AND past-cutoff rows still remaining. Zero-deleted ALONE is the normal steady state once the backlog is drained, so alerting on it would fire every night forever, which is exactly how a channel becomes noise and stops being read (the same reasoning behind the cron-fleet suppression window in US-2004). Escalation is by CONSECUTIVE RUNS rather than elapsed time, because the failure is 'the sweep is not advancing' and runs are the unit in which that is true: one odd run is a warning, three consecutive is critical. The streak is carried on the ops event payload and read back next run, mirroring the loadLastAlert pattern already used by jobs-cron-fleet rather than inventing a second mechanism. decideRetentionStall is pure with 5 tests; the whole check is best-effort in a try/catch for the same stated reason as the prunes beside it — the stall DETECTOR must never be the reason the purge itself reports failure. NEGATIVE-VERIFIED by weakening the conjunction to a bare zero-check (the tempting simplification): the 'nothing left to do is NOT a stall' test goes red, which is the assertion standing between this alert and nightly noise. Also aligned the severity vocabulary to ops-events' 'warning' rather than casting my own 'warn' through — a cast would have compiled and produced an event severity nothing downstream ranks. Verified: edge 4278 passed, deno check + lint clean. STILL OPEN: AC3 alone — quantify and drain the backlog of past-retention imagery that accumulated while the sweep was stalled. That needs prod DB access, and note the new alert will now TELL you the size of that backlog on the next run (past_cutoff_remaining in the event payload), so AC3 gets its number for free once this deploys.

userStories.title: Migration tracking is a max-watermark, so a skipped mid-sequence migration is undetectable — this already happened
userStories.description: As GradeThread, we want to know EVERY migration applied, not just the highest-numbered one. latest_schema_migration() (00254:63-79) returns GREATEST(max(cli), max(self)); apply-prod-migrations.sh:29-31 skips any file whose prefix is <= current; schema-version.ts:41 compares a single number. A gap in the MIDDLE of the range is structurally invisible — the watermark only moves forward and a file below it is never re-applied. 00254:108-111 even seeds 00252/00253 on the assumption that reaching 00254 means 00250..00253 ran. NOT THEORETICAL: 00322_api_keys_webhook_url_idempotent.sql:1-16 documents the realized incident — 00005's non-idempotent ADD COLUMN webhook_url never landed in prod, the watermark advanced anyway, and EVERY finalized grade silently no-op'd its developer webhook delivery with 42703 for an unknown duration.
acceptanceCriteria: Change the boot guard from a watermark comparison to a COMPLETENESS check: ship the expected version set as a manifest in the edge image and fail on any missing version, not just on max.

Run a one-time prod-vs-migrations COLUMN-LEVEL diff (information_schema.columns against the parsed corpus). No such check exists today, and it is the only thing that would have caught webhook_url. The ~253 pre-00254 files carry no self-record footer, so any could have partially failed the same way.
Note post-00254 hygiene is already excellent — all 224 files >= 00254 carry the footer, zero exceptions — so this is about the historical tail, not new work.
userStories.notes: [P2][DB/Ops] Found 2026-07-18 by the data-integrity deep dive, dovetailing with a measurement made the same day: /health/ready reports schema {expected:00476, applied:00476, status:match}, which proves the MAX is current and proves nothing about intermediate versions. That is exactly the residual risk here. Re-running the tail via apply-prod-migrations.sh is idempotent and remains the cheap mitigation; the manifest check is the durable one. | 2026-07-19 AC1 DONE; AC2 needs prod DB access. The boot guard is no longer a watermark comparison. scripts/gen-migration-manifest.mjs generates lib/migration-manifest.ts (231 footer-era versions) into the edge image, and checkSchemaCompleteness() reads the WHOLE applied set and reports two opposite findings: MISSING (in the manifest, never applied — the mid-sequence gap a max comparison structurally cannot see, since the watermark only moves forward and apply-prod-migrations.sh skips anything at or below it) and UNEXPECTED (recorded in applied_migrations with no migration file in this build). MANIFEST STARTS AT 00254 DELIBERATELY: the self-recording footer was introduced by that migration, so the ~253 files below it legitimately do not self-record and their absence carries no signal. Including them would emit ~253 permanent false 'missing' reports, and a check that always fires is a check nobody reads. THE UNEXPECTED DIRECTION IS NOT HYPOTHETICAL AND IS WHY I BUILT IT THIS WAY: measured live this session, /health/ready reports applied=00479 while NO 00479 file has ever existed in this repo. That is the exact phantom this half detects, and it is the reason 00480-00485 were numbered around it — reusing 00479 would have satisfied the boot guard off a stale row even if the SQL never ran, which is the precise failure the guard exists to prevent. On the next edge deploy the container log will NAME the phantom, which answers PENDING_MIGRATIONS.md's open question 1 without a psql session; I noted that there. DELIBERATELY NON-FATAL, unlike the behind-max check, and this is the judgement to review: it is a brand-new assertion over 231 historical migrations that has NEVER run against prod. If any one of them failed to self-record years ago, making it fatal would refuse to boot the whole service on the first deploy containing this code — converting an unknown into an outage, which is the same trap I avoided in US-2003 (declined to fail at boot on a missing alert channel). It logs at ERROR instead. PROMOTE IT TO FATAL once prod is observed clean; that is a deliberate follow-up, not an oversight. Fails CLOSED in the sense that matters: a read error returns checked:false, which must never render as 'clean'. 6 tests including the mid-sequence gap where the MAX still matches (the case the old guard could not see) and the 00479 phantom as a literal case, plus a drift guard asserting the generated manifest matches supabase/migrations on disk — otherwise adding a migration without regenerating would silently shrink what the guard checks. AC2 (one-time prod-vs-migrations COLUMN-LEVEL diff against information_schema) still needs DB access and remains the only thing that would catch a migration that applied PARTIALLY. Verified: edge 4272 passed, deno check + lint clean.

userStories.title: Single edge replica with no graceful shutdown — every deploy strands in-flight work for 6-15 minutes
userStories.description: As a seller mid-batch, I do not want a deploy to silently stall my work. SCALING.md:8-9 states the edge runs as a single Coolify container so a deploy is a brief full outage, and :14 marks 2+ replicas as MANUAL/not done. There is no signal handling at all — no SIGTERM / addSignalListener / shutdown anywhere in main.ts (1638 lines) — so in-flight requests are KILLED, not drained. Recovery is by sweep rather than drain: flipdesk-autolister.ts:114 JOB_STALE_MS = 6min, :117 BATCH_STALE_MS = 15min, reclaim crons at */5. The ~30s outage documented at SCALING.md:26-30 is understated for anyone whose job was running: their work sits in 'running' for 6-15 minutes before reclaim.
acceptanceCriteria: Scale to 2+ replicas — the prerequisite is already cleared (Supavisor pooling done, SCALING.md:22).
Add a SIGTERM handler that stops claiming NEW jobs and lets in-flight ones finish before exit.
Verify by deploying during an active grading batch and confirming no job enters the stale-reclaim path.
userStories.notes:
[P2][Ops/Reliability] Found 2026-07-18 by the operational-readiness deep dive. Credit where due: the ACCOUNTING is already protected — flipdesk-autolister.ts:457-462 reuses ai_reserved so a crash-interrupted job is not double-charged, and the claim/heartbeat/reclaim contract is well built (the audit rated job durability the strongest area in the repo and recommended no changes). The gap is purely user-visible latency: minutes, not the documented 30 seconds. | 2026-07-19 AC2 DONE; AC1/AC3 need Coolify + a deploy. New lib/lifecycle.ts installs SIGTERM/SIGINT handlers that stop claiming NEW work immediately and drain in-flight requests before exit (SHUTDOWN_DRAIN_MS, default 8s — deliberately INSIDE Docker's 10s SIGTERM-to-SIGKILL grace, since a drain deadline longer than the grace period is a drain that gets killed halfway having already stopped claiming). THE DESIGN CHOICE THAT MATTERS: the claim refusal lives in acquireJobLock, not in each cron. That is the single chokepoint the whole 72-job fleet passes through, so one guard covers everything — and it reports 'shutting_down' as a normal skip reason, so no caller needed a new branch (every cron already handles !acquired). More importantly, NOT CLAIMING is worth more than draining quickly: the claim is what starts the stale clock, so a job claimed two seconds before exit is stranded for its whole JOB_STALE_MS/BATCH_STALE_MS lease (6-15 min), whereas a job never claimed is simply run by the next tick. Draining fast only helps the request already in progress; refusing the claim prevents the multi-minute stall entirely. 10 tests. ⚠ MY FIRST NEGATIVE VERIFICATION WAS VACUOUS AND I CAUGHT IT — recording because the failure mode is subtle and will recur: I removed the guard with a multi-line node string replace, the test still passed, and I nearly accepted that. The file is CRLF (enforced by .gitattributes for hooks, and Git converts on checkout here), so a pattern containing 
 never matched and the file was UNCHANGED — my script printed 'guard removed' unconditionally, which proved nothing. Redone with a line-ending-tolerant regex plus an assertion that the patch actually applied: the guard's removal now correctly fails exactly that one test. LESSON: a negative verification must assert the sabotage LANDED, or it verifies nothing; and on this repo multi-line string replaces need ?
. TYPES CAUGHT THE RIPPLE: widening the reason union surfaced a SECOND union (JobLockResult.skipped) that would otherwise have silently diverged. Also corrected vault/10-ops/scaling.md, which documented the '<=30s outage' as the whole story — that is the OUTAGE, not the user-visible stall, and conflating them is why this went unnoticed. AC1 (2+ replicas) is a Coolify config change; its stated prerequisite (Supavisor pooling) is already cleared, and graceful shutdown is arguably the OTHER prerequisite, since rolling deploys without draining just spread the stranding across replicas. AC3 needs a deploy during an active batch. NOT A REPLACEMENT FOR THE SWEEPS, and the note says so: SIGKILL/OOM/host loss bypass all of this, so the reclaim crons remain the correctness backstop; this only improves the orderly case, which is every routine deploy. Verified: edge 4254 passed, deno check + lint clean.

userStories.notes: [P2][Ops/Payments] Found 2026-07-18 by the operational-readiness deep dive. Smallest fix-to-impact ratio in the audit: one line converts silent revenue loss into a page. Blocked in practice on the alert-channel story (setting the webhook secrets), since the fan-out currently has nowhere to go. | 2026-07-18 FIXED (agent loop). recordWebhookDeadLetter now emits a CRITICAL ops event alongside the existing captureException, so a dropped webhook reaches the on-call fan-out instead of only Sentry (whose routing is separately unverified — US-2003). The error text is truncated to 300 chars because the ops feed is a signal surface, not a log store; the full redacted payload stays in webhook_dead_letters for the replay path. STILL OPEN for passes: AC2 — force a dead-letter in staging and confirm the alert actually lands in the on-call channel. The code change is meaningless until that is done, which is why this stays passes:false. | 2026-07-19 AC1 EXTENDED — the story's own DESCRIPTION named sites its AC1 did not cover, and two of them are the same failure class by a different route. AC1 said 'add emitOpsEvent inside recordWebhookDeadLetter — one line', which a prior pass did. But the description also cited 'routes/webhooks.ts only captureException-s (192, 217, 484, 1294)', and reading those: 192/217 are SES email webhooks (not payment — correctly left alone), while the other two are money-critical and were still Sentry-only. (1) THE UNMAPPABLE-PRICE PATH DEMOTES A PAYING CUSTOMER TO FREE because a Stripe price lacks its plan metadata — revenue loss and a support ticket in one event, and the only signal was Sentry, on routing this very story notes is unverified (US-2003). (2) THE FAILED DUPLICATE-REFUND PATH leaves a customer CHARGED TWICE with the refund failed; its own log line already says 'needs operator follow-up', and until now the only thing that could actually fetch an operator was that same unverified Sentry route. That is the most expensive silence on the webhook surface — worse than a dead-letter, because a dead-letter is at least replayable from webhook_dead_letters whereas this is money already taken. Both now emit CRITICAL ops events. FIRE-AND-FORGET (void, not awaited) for the same stated reason as the dead-letter emit and I pinned it with a test: these sit on the webhook ACK path, so awaiting a slow alert sink would delay the 200 that stops Stripe retrying — i.e. the alert about a webhook problem would itself cause the retry storm. The duplicate-refund error text is truncated to 300 chars because the ops feed is a signal surface, not a log store. 3 tests, source-asserted (these handlers talk to Stripe and the service-role client with no injection seam, so the property worth pinning — 'does this path reach the on-call fan-out at all' — is visible in the source). NEGATIVE-VERIFIED both directions: deleting the unmappable-price emit and switching an emit from void to await each turn the suite red. userStories.notes: [P2][Security/Testing] Found 2026-07-18 by the security deep dive. CRITICAL CONTEXT so this is not misread as a breach: the audit traced all 740 .from() call sites on multi-tenant tables, taint-traced request-supplied ids into filters, and machine-diffed every mounted route against the middleware tables — and could NOT confirm a single cross-tenant data hole. Every unscoped-LOOKING query hand-verified as parent-verified (inventory_items!inner(user_id), loadListingOwned, loadReconcilePair, or a locally-minted id). The US-268 discipline is genuinely being followed. This story closes the TEST gap and inverts a default that currently makes unauthenticated exposure a silent one-line mistake. | 2026-07-18 THREE OF FOUR ACs (agent loop). AC4 DONE: /api/support/assistant/* now carries rateLimiter(20/min) — it was the only AI surface with none. Not an open faucet before (support-assistant.ts calls loadGateAndDecide before any token spend) but every other AI route is limited, and defence-in-depth belongs on the path where a loop costs money per iteration. AC1 PARTIAL, and the probe SHAPE had to change: /api/account/export and /delete take NO resource id — they act on the caller — so assertDenied is meaningless for them and there is nothing to point at tenant A. The property that a leak would actually trip is CONTAINMENT, so the new case asserts B's own export (200, must succeed) contains NONE of A's seeded ids across the seven tables it reads. Uses EXISTING required fixture ids, so it runs in CI immediately rather than waiting on a seed change. Also added an env-gated remove-bg probe (that route writes to the PUBLIC item-photos bucket, so a cross-tenant call would publish another seller's photo) — deliberately NOT added to REQUIRED_RESOURCE_IDS, because a case that hard-fails CI before the seed script provides TEST_USER_A_PHOTO_ID would simply get muted, which is worse than skipping loudly. Plus an unauthenticated-read probe on equity. ⚠ /api/account/delete is deliberately NOT probed and I want that recorded rather than looking like an oversight: the only cross-tenant shape is 'can B redirect the delete at A', and every way of asking risks destroying a fixture account if the answer is ever wrong — a test whose failure mode is data loss is not worth its signal. The route reads only c.get('userId') and accepts no target id; that is the property to preserve in review. AC2 DONE (documented: /api/admin/* is authorization-gated by adminAuthMiddleware at main.ts:730-731, so it is lower priority by design, not by neglect). AC3 — I DELIBERATELY DID NOT DO WHAT THE AC ASKED, and this is the judgement call to review. The AC says invert to app.use('/api/flipdesk/ebay/*', authMiddleware) + skip-list. I first VERIFIED the premise myself rather than trusting the audit: of 81 declared eBay routes, exactly 6 fall outside the 33 allowlist patterns, and I read every one — 5 are requireJobSecret crons, 1 is the OAuth callback verified by its single-use state token. So there is NO live gap, confirming the audit independently. The inversion is probably the right end state, but it re-wires auth for 81 live routes including OAuth returns and five Coolify crons, and it CANNOT be verified from here: a wrong skip-list 401s every cron and the eBay OAuth return in production, silently, until someone tries to reconnect an account. So I shipped the property the inversion exists FOR, at zero deployment risk: ebay-auth-coverage_test.ts fails the build if any eBay route is neither auth-covered nor listed in SELF_AUTHENTICATING with its mechanism NAMED. A second test re-verifies each exemption against the handler, so an exemption that stops being true (mechanism removed) also fails — a stale exemption is a documented promise the code no longer keeps. NEGATIVE-VERIFIED by injecting an unauthenticated GET /secret-seller-report: the guard names it and fails; removing it passes. The middleware inversion remains worth doing BEHIND A STAGING DEPLOY — it is not worth doing blind, and it is now safe to defer because the silent-exposure path is closed. Verified: deno check + lint clean, 4169 edge tests pass. userStories.title: Android is a plumbing skeleton, but its README and 19 passing stories claim near-parity
userStories.description: As GradeThread, we want the Android backlog to reflect reality. It has no product: every navigation destination except one is a literal placeholder (ui/shell/AppShell.kt:162-175 — Home, Inventory, Money, Marketplaces, Settings, Details intake, AutoLister all render SectionPlaceholder; only capture/photos is real). Corroborating: Android calls exactly ONE edge endpoint in the entire codebase (/api/flipdesk/photo-profiles) versus iOS's 77 and web's ~530 — no grading submit, no inventory read, no eBay, no payments. Two documentation problems compound it: android/README.md:31-39 presents a package map for grading / inventory / marketplaces / money / billing whose directories contain ZERO .kt files, and :3 calls it 'at iOS parity'. And 19 stories are marked passes:true with no implementing code — verified: US-1380 Glance widgets (zero 'glance' references anywhere, no AppWidgetProvider in the manifest), US-1378 FCM push (no FirebaseMessaging reference), US-1383 Settings (routes to a placeholder), US-1384/1385/1387/1388/1389, US-1393 localization (no values-* locale dirs). acceptanceCriteria: Re-open the falsely-passing Android stories (start with the verified list: US-1380, US-1378, US-1383, US-1384, US-1385, US-1387, US-1388, US-1389, US-1393) and audit the rest of the US-1378-1396 block the same way.

userStories.title: iOS silently omits the entire paid consumer grading path, including the 14-day dispute flow
userStories.description: As a consumer grading on iOS, I want the same journey the web offers. There are TWO independent grading pipelines in the edge: the consumer/certified path (routes/grade.ts:209 /submit, :751 /pay/:id, :837 /status/:id, :1117 /dispute) and the FlipDesk/reseller path (/api/flipdesk/grading/{validate,submit,submissions/:id}). Web implements BOTH (new-submission.tsx:647, bulk-submission.tsx:332, submission-detail.tsx:244). iOS implements ONLY the FlipDesk path — Grading/GradingService.swift:6,55 documents and calls validate -> submit -> GET /submissions/:id — and grepping iOS for grade/pay, grade/status and grade/dispute returns NOTHING. So iOS has no consumer certified-grading submission, no per-grade payment flow, and NO GRADE DISPUTE FLOW at all.
acceptanceCriteria: Decide explicitly whether the consumer grading path belongs on iOS. Nothing in IOS_PARITY_AUDIT.md or the Android plan mentions this omission either way, which is weak evidence it is accidental rather than a product decision — settle it in writing.
If it belongs: implement submit / pay / status / dispute on iOS against routes/grade.ts.

If it does not: document why, and confirm the dispute obligation is discharged some other way — a 14-day dispute window that only one client can exercise is a support and chargeback liability regardless of intent.
Any parity matrix must stop treating 'grading submission' as ONE row; scoring it that way marks iOS complete while the entire paid consumer path is missing.
userStories.notes: [P1][iOS/Parity] Found 2026-07-18 by the cross-platform parity deep dive. Two implementations of the core revenue journey is the highest-value drift surface in the repo, and the mobile client omits the paid half. The dispute gap is the sharpest edge: US-1340 tracks a 14-day dispute window as a real obligation, and a user who graded on iOS has no in-app route to exercise it.

userStories.title: Legal ToS/privacy versions are hardcoded in both clients while the server derives them from the DB — and iOS has no re-acceptance gate
userStories.description: As GradeThread, we want consent records to name the version the user actually saw. The edge derives current legal versions DYNAMICALLY from DB rows (lib/legal-versions.ts:66, consumed at routes/legal.ts:73,105,162). Both clients HARDCODE them: ios/GradeThread/Auth/AuthStore.swift:19-20 (legalTosVersion / legalPrivacyVersion = '2026-04-01') and src/lib/constants.ts:1491-1494 (LEGAL_VERSIONS). The only sync mechanism is a code comment (AuthStore.swift:17-18, 'Keep IN SYNC with the web ... and the edge mirror') with no automated guard. Worse, iOS has NO re-acceptance gate at all: web has src/components/auth/legal-gate.tsx; iOS never calls /api/legal (0 matches).
acceptanceCriteria: Clients must READ the current version from the server rather than hardcoding it, or a build-time guard must fail when the constants disagree with the DB-backed source.
Implement a re-acceptance gate on iOS equivalent to legal-gate.tsx.
Add a test/guard covering the three-way agreement (edge DB, web constants, iOS constants) — a comment is not a mechanism.
userStories.notes: [P1][Compliance/Legal] Found 2026-07-18 by the cross-platform parity deep dive. The failure mode is silent and legally material: the moment an operator publishes a new ToS row via admin-legal.ts, web and iOS signups keep recording 2026-04-01 — users are attested to a version they were never shown, and iOS users are never re-prompted at all. That is a defensible-consent failure, and exactly what an enterprise or legal review looks for. | 2026-07-18 SCOPED DOWN + GUARD ADDED (agent loop). ⚠ THIS STORY OVERSTATED THE RISK and the correction matters more than the fix. It claims users are 'attested to a version they were never shown'. For the WEB that is not what happens: legal-gate.tsx does NOT trust the hardcoded constant — it asks /api/legal/status (its own comment says so at :29) — and /api/legal/accept stamps the SERVER's current versions (legal.ts:103-106), never a client-supplied value. So after a FORCING republish the system SELF-CORRECTS: the gate fires and an immutable legal_acceptances row is written with the real version. The genuine residual hole is narrower and does NOT self-correct: on a MINOR republish (requires_reacceptance:false) requiredSince deliberately does not advance, so the gate correctly stays quiet — while handle_new_user (00142:79) still records the CLIENT-SUPPLIED constant into users.tos_accepted_version. The new user was shown the live document (/terms serves current) but their record names an older version, and nothing later corrects it. Moderate, not the defensible-consent failure described. FIXED WHAT IS FIXABLE HERE: added src/lib/__tests__/legal-versions-lockstep.test.ts pinning the baseline across all THREE projects that hold it — web LEGAL_VERSIONS, edge FALLBACK_TOS/PRIVACY_VERSION, and iOS AuthStore.legalTosVersion/legalPrivacyVersion — plus a shape check so a placeholder value cannot silently disable the gate. NEGATIVE-VERIFIED from every direction: drifting the web constant fails 2 assertions, drifting the iOS constant fails 1. That iOS assertion is the valuable one — Swift cannot be compiled on a Windows checkout, so a source-level check is the ONLY cross-project verification available for it. STILL passing:false on the two real ACs: (1) the durable fix is for the server to stamp the version at signup rather than trusting client metadata — that is a migration to handle_new_user and I did not want to stack a third held one; (2) iOS still has NO re-acceptance gate at all (grep for api/legal across ios/ returns nothing), which remains the largest genuine gap in this story and needs a macOS session. [2026-07-19 AC3 DONE + AC1 GUARD HALF. AC2 NEEDS macOS — story stays open] AC3 was the whole point of the story (a comment is not a mechanism) and is now real: src/test/legal-version-parity.test.ts asserts the THREE-WAY agreement between the edge fallbacks (FALLBACK_TOS_VERSION / FALLBACK_PRIVACY_VERSION), web LEGAL_VERSIONS, and the iOS AuthStore.swift static lets, by parsing each source. Negative-verified by bumping the iOS constant to 2026-09-01 — the guard fails naming all three values. AC1: took the guard option the AC explicitly allows rather than making clients read /api/legal at runtime. A build-time comparison against the live DB is not possible (no DB at build), and the edge FALLBACK constants are the DB-backed sources checked-in form, so this pins what CAN be pinned. Making the clients dynamic remains the stronger fix and is still open. Also asserted the versions are ISO dates: the edge ORDERS versions to decide whether re-acceptance is required, so a free-form string would break that comparison silently. And the parse-succeeded guard is explicit, because comparing null to null would have passed vacuously — it caught a real bug immediately when a heredoc ate the backslashes in my regex and both parsers returned null. AC2 NOT DONE and deliberately not faked: iOS has no re-acceptance gate (never calls /api/legal) while web has legal-gate.tsx. I cannot build or test Swift on Windows, and writing a compliance gate blind is precisely the wrong place for that. A test asserts the gap STILL EXISTS so it flips the moment someone implements it, rather than the story looking complete because the parity guard is green. AuthStore.swift now documents the gap in place. Seventh prose-matching guard failure this session: my new Swift comment names /api/legal, which the absence assertion matched. Comments are stripped now. | 2026-07-19 ⚠ STALE HELD-MIGRATION CLAIM — do not act on it. The migration(s) this note calls HELD (00142) are all on origin/main, verified individually with git log origin/main against each file rather than inferred from the linter's summary. The standing rule makes this decisive: a commit containing a migration is NOT pushed until the operator has applied the SQL, so a migration present on origin/main was pushed, which means its hold was already released. PENDING_MIGRATIONS.md agrees — every entry through 00490 (the highest migration in the tree) is marked APPLIED and confirmed by the user, so nothing is genuinely pending. WHY THIS MATTERS ENOUGH TO CORRECT: a stale hold tells the next reader the branch is frozen when it is not, which either invites a pointless prod session or — worse — makes them hold back an unrelated push that was always safe. Correction APPENDED rather than edited into the original sentence, because these notes are append-only and the history of what was believed when is itself worth keeping.

userStories.title: email_deliveries stores full rendered email bodies forever with no purge
userStories.description: As GradeThread, we want the email log bounded. 00095_email_deliveries.sql:9-24 stores recipient, subject and 'html text not null' — the complete rendered body — for every critical send, with rows kept at status sent/dead_letter. There is NO purge anywhere: the only pruning in lib/data-retention.ts:132 is cron_runs (30-day window). No DELETE FROM email_deliveries exists in the codebase.
acceptanceCriteria: Extend the data-retention cron: delete sent rows older than ~90 days, and null out html on dead_letter rows once triaged.
Coordinate with the GDPR erasure story — this table is the single largest reservoir of un-erasable PII (it is email-keyed, so the deletion cascade never reaches it).

Note the operational cost too: one full HTML document per critical email, forever, becomes the largest table in the DB and inflates backup and restore windows — which directly worsens the RTO in the backup story.
userStories.notes: [P3][DB/Growth] Found 2026-07-18 by the data-integrity deep dive. Compounds three other findings at once: GDPR erasure (un-erasable PII), backup/restore duration (RTO), and the stalled retention sweep (the cron that would own this purge is itself not advancing). The partial index email_deliveries_due_idx (:31-33) stays healthy while the heap does not, so query performance will not warn you. | 2026-07-18 FIXED (agent loop). AC1 DONE, with TWO DIFFERENT RULES rather than the one the AC implied — the distinction matters and is the whole risk of this change: (1) status='sent' rows are pure history once delivered, so they are DELETED after 90 days (well past any support window that would need to re-read what a user was actually sent); (2) status='dead_letter' rows are an OPERATOR REPLAY QUEUE and are NEVER deleted — only their heavy PII-bearing `html` body is stripped, and on a longer 180-day window so a genuine replay stays possible. Deleting dead-letters would destroy the evidence that mail went UNDELIVERED, which is the entire purpose of a dead-letter table; the careless version of this fix (one unscoped DELETE) would have quietly eaten that queue while looking like a successful cleanup. Both cutoffs are named constants with the reasoning inline. Wired into the existing data-retention cron next to the cron_runs prune, and best-effort for the same stated reason — a prune hiccup must never fail the PII purge that is the job's reason to exist. THREE NEW TESTS in data-retention_test.ts, all NEGATIVE-VERIFIED by simulating the exact careless edits: removing .eq('status','sent') fails the scoping test, and switching the dead-letter .update({html:''}) to .delete() fails the body-strip test; restoring passes. Checked against the repo gotcha too — no .or() on an UPDATE/DELETE (US-1552), only .eq/.lt/.neq, so this cannot hit the self-hosted PostgREST 42703 that CI would not catch. Verified: deno check + lint clean, 4167 edge tests pass. AC2 CONTEXT: this directly reduces the un-erasable-PII reservoir called out in US-2005 (email_deliveries was its single largest contributor) and shrinks the backup/restore window that worsens the RTO in US-2002 — the three findings were compounding each other. STILL passes:false on AC3's quantification: how much this actually reclaims, and how much accumulated while there was no purge at all, needs a prod query (select pg_total_relation_size('public.email_deliveries'), count(*) filter (where status='sent' and created_at < now() - interval '90 days')). Worth running BEFORE the first sweep so the reclaim is measured rather than assumed, and worth knowing that the first run will be a large delete on a table nobody has ever pruned. | 2026-07-19 FOLLOW-UP: THE SWEEP IS NOW BOUNDED. AC1 shipped previously and AC2 is satisfied (email_deliveries IS covered by the account-delete email-keyed purge at account.ts:564, so the un-erasable reservoir is addressed from both ends). What the previous pass flagged in its own closing line but did not fix: 'the first run will be a large delete on a table nobody has ever pruned'. That was left as an unbounded DELETE over the entire historical backlog — a long transaction and a WAL spike on what is on track to be the largest table in the DB, running in a nightly cron on a SINGLE-REPLICA edge with no graceful shutdown until today. Both sweeps now select at most EMAIL_PURGE_BATCH (5,000) ids and mutate by id. A capped run is not a lost run: the cron is daily, so a backlog drains over consecutive nights and each night's work stays predictable. IMPLEMENTED AS scan-then-mutate-by-id RATHER THAN A LIMIT ON THE MUTATION, deliberately: per the US-1552 gotcha, the self-hosted prod PostgREST and the newer local stack disagree about what they accept on UPDATE/DELETE, so CI structurally cannot catch a regression there — two plain statements are version-proof. The run now also REPORTS what it did (email_sent_purged / email_bodies_stripped / email_purge_batch), because a capped run that reports nothing is indistinguishable from a no-op, and those counts are how an operator knows whether the backlog is still draining. REWROTE TWO EXISTING TESTS RATHER THAN LOOSENING THEM: they asserted the old source shape (.update chained directly to .eq) which the batching necessarily changed. The INTENT was right and is preserved — scoping is now asserted on the SCAN, which is the same property since the mutation only ever receives ids that query produced — plus a new test that both sweeps carry the cap. NEGATIVE-VERIFIED all three by simulating the exact careless edits: removing the limits, unscoping the sent purge, and switching the dead-letter strip to a delete each turn the suite red; restoring returns it to zero. STILL passes:false on AC3 alone: how much this reclaims needs a prod query (select pg_total_relation_size('public.email_deliveries'), count(*) filter (where status='sent' and created_at < now() - interval '90 days')), and it is worth running BEFORE the first sweep so the reclaim is measured rather than assumed. Verified: edge 4273 passed, deno check + lint clean.

userStories.title: GDPR data export materializes a seller's entire commercial history in one isolate
userStories.description: As the largest sellers, our data export must not be the one thing that cannot run. services/edge-functions/src/routes/account.ts:221-227 selects grade_reports (.in submissionIds), listings (.eq user_id) and sales (.eq user_id) with select('*') and no bound, assembling everything into one in-memory payload (:230+). Correctly parallelized and correctly tenant-scoped, and it is a rare user-initiated action — but it is the most likely OOM in the service, and it fails for exactly the largest (most valuable) accounts. Same file :378-381 fetches submissions.select('id') and inventory_items.select('id') purely to COUNT them; duplicated at admin-compliance.ts:474 and lib/support-tools.ts:77,96,396.
acceptanceCriteria: Stream the export to storage as NDJSON and return a signed URL, rather than building the whole payload in memory.
Replace the count-by-fetching-ids patterns with count:'exact', head:true.
Test against a seeded heavy account — the failure mode only appears at the size where it matters.
userStories.notes: [P3][Perf/Compliance] Found 2026-07-18 by the query-performance deep dive. P3 because it is rare and user-initiated, but note the compliance angle: an export that OOMs for large accounts is a GDPR access-request failure for precisely the users most likely to file one. Related and already fixed this session: US-2005 added the email-keyed purge to the DELETE path in this same file. | 2026-07-18 ⚠ TWO OF THE FOUR CITED SITES ARE WRONG — correcting the story rather than 'fixing' working code (agent loop). The audit claimed account.ts:378-381 and admin-compliance.ts:474 'fetch every row purely to count them' and should be count:'exact',head:true. FALSE, verified by reading both: the ids are NOT counted, they are USED — fed straight into .in('submission_id', subIds) / .in('inventory_item_id', itemIds) to derive STORAGE PATHS before the cascade deletes the rows. Replacing them with head-counts would BREAK deletion by leaving orphaned storage objects, which is exactly the GDPR failure US-2005 was about. A head:true count returns no rows at all. support-tools.ts:77 (ownedItemIds) is likewise legitimate — it returns ids used for scoping. The ONE genuine instance is support-tools.ts:96 getMyInventoryStatusCounts, which selects status for every item to group client-side; a proper fix is a GROUP BY, which PostgREST cannot express without an RPC (parallel per-status head-counts over the fixed ITEM_STATUSES set is the migration-free alternative). Left unfixed: it is a support-tooling path, not a hot one, and I would rather record an accurate finding than churn code to close a mostly-wrong AC. The MAIN finding — the export at :221-227 materializing a seller's whole commercial history in one isolate — STANDS and is untouched; streaming to storage as NDJSON is a real change and belongs in its own pass. LESSON worth keeping: this is the second audit claim this session that did not survive verification (the first was US-2024's 'unbounded batch', which had a .max(200) all along). Read the code before acting on a finding, even a well-argued one. | 2026-07-19 AC1 DONE (the main finding); AC2 was already correctly REJECTED by the prior pass; AC3 still needs a seeded heavy account. The export no longer materializes a seller's whole commercial history in one isolate: grade_reports, listings and sales are now PAGED (500 rows/round trip) and written progressively to a streamed response, so peak memory is ~one page per table instead of the account. The small inherently-bounded sets (profile, sources, passport nodes) stay eager — paging a handful of rows buys nothing and costs clarity. TWO DELIBERATE DEVIATIONS FROM AC1, both argued rather than convenient. (1) NOT TO STORAGE: writing a subject's complete personal-data export to a bucket creates a NEW COPY OF THEIR DATA AT REST, which then carries its own retention and deletion obligation — a GDPR storage-limitation problem manufactured by a GDPR access-request fix — plus a signed-URL lifecycle to get wrong. Streaming the response creates no copy and needs no new bucket, which also means no seventh held migration. (2) NOT NDJSON: ios/GradeThread/Settings/AccountExportService.swift consumes this endpoint as RAW BYTES and writes them to gradethread-export.json. NDJSON was presumably chosen because it streams naturally, but a JSON document streams just as well written progressively, and keeping the shape preserves the existing client contract exactly — changing the bytes inside a .json file is a silent break for anything that parses it. The property that actually mattered (never hold the whole account in memory) is delivered either way. THE ERROR PATH GOT THE MOST THOUGHT: once headers are sent a mid-stream failure cannot become a 500, so the stream is ERRORED rather than closed. A truncated-but-valid-looking JSON file is the worst possible outcome here — the subject receives something that LOOKS complete and is not, a compliance failure disguised as a success — whereas an aborted download is visibly broken. Same reasoning makes pageThrough THROW on a page error instead of returning what it has. 9 tests on the pure helpers covering the boundaries that only bite at scale: an exact multiple of the page size (the off-by-one that would drop or duplicate a page), a short first page terminating in ONE query, an empty table, and a mid-page error. Comma placement is verified by PARSING the assembled envelope back for both an empty and a populated account, since a stray comma produces invalid JSON only when a section is non-empty — precisely what a small test account would not catch. AC3 (verify against a seeded heavy account) remains genuinely undone: the failure mode only appears at the size where it matters, and I have no such account. Verified: edge 4265 passed, deno check + lint clean.

userStories.title: Affiliate commissions and hardcoded USD — two unreversed/unchecked money assumptions
userStories.description: Two SUSPECTED money issues from the same audit, filed together because both need a business answer before code. (1) AFFILIATE CLAWBACK: lib/affiliate-payout.ts has a hold_until window (default 30 days, affiliate-payout-math.ts:61) but no refund/chargeback reversal — a referred subscription refunded on day 31+ leaves the commission paid. Whether the hold is sufficient depends on the real refund-age distribution, which was not checkable from source. (2) CURRENCY: consignor-payout.ts:325 hardcodes currency 'usd' with Math.round(amount * 100). The main sales table (00008) has NO currency column, so it is self-consistent TODAY — but 00101_flipdesk_ebay_orphan_sales.sql:21 and 00327_ebay_payouts.sql:14 DO carry currency, and flipdesk-ebay.ts:1955 defaults line items to 'USD'. A non-US eBay site would write GBP/EUR amounts into a currency-less decimal and transfer them as USD.
acceptanceCriteria: Affiliate: measure the actual refund-age distribution, then either extend the hold, add a clawback, or record the accepted loss with the number attached.

Currency: decide whether non-US marketplaces are in scope. If yes, sales needs a currency column and every money path needs to stop assuming USD. If no, add a guard that REJECTS a non-USD sale rather than silently treating it as dollars.
Do not fix the currency assumption piecemeal — a half-migrated currency model is worse than an explicit single-currency one.
userStories.notes: [P2][Money] Found 2026-07-18 by the money deep dive, both filed as SUSPECTED rather than confirmed. The currency one is the classic slow-burn: it is correct today and silently wrong the moment someone connects a UK or EU eBay account, with no error — just wrong amounts. Also captured from the same audit, not filed separately: ai-metering.ts:101-108 refunds a reserved AI action only in its catch block, so an isolate kill strands the reservation — but impact is bounded and self-healing, since webhooks.ts:868-877 zeroes ai_actions_used_this_month each cycle. Worth knowing, not worth a story. | 2026-07-19 CURRENCY HALF DONE (AC2); AFFILIATE HALF (AC1) STILL NEEDS A BUSINESS ANSWER. The AC offered two routes and named the fallback itself: support multi-currency, or REJECT a non-USD sale rather than silently treat it as dollars. Took the reject route, because it needs no business decision, forecloses neither option, and converts a silent wrongness into a loud refusal. WHAT MADE THIS NON-TRIVIAL: to reject you must first DETECT, and the sales table had no currency column at all — which is exactly why the USD assumption was invisible rather than merely wrong. eBay reports the currency per line item and the orphan-sales path already stored it (flipdesk-ebay.ts:1958); the MAIN sales row discarded it. So migration 00484 adds sales.currency, the eBay sync now records what eBay actually told us, and processSaleConsignorPayout refuses + raises a CRITICAL ops event when it is anything other than USD. DELIBERATELY NOT A PARTIAL MULTI-CURRENCY MODEL — the AC warns a half-migrated currency model is worse than an explicit single-currency one, and it is right. Nothing converts amounts; no other money path learns about currencies; the column exists solely as the guard's input. NULLABLE WITH NO BACKFILL, which is the judgement worth recording: NULL means 'the marketplace never told us' and is treated as USD, so every pre-existing sale behaves exactly as before. Defaulting the column to 'USD' would have been the tempting shape and would have FABRICATED a fact we do not have, making a genuinely-unknown currency indistinguishable from a confirmed-USD one. Pinned by 3 tests including the legacy-NULL case, since the failure mode of over-strict enforcement here is refusing to pay consignors on every historical sale. AC1 (affiliate clawback) UNTOUCHED and still correctly blocked: it asks to measure the real refund-age distribution before choosing between extending the hold, adding a clawback, or accepting the loss — that is a prod-data question plus a business call, not a code change. Note the consignor engine now HAS the clawback affiliate lacks (US-2022), so if the answer is 'add one', consignor-payout.ts reverseConsignorPayoutsForSales is the working precedent to copy. Verified: edge 4226 passed, deno check + lint clean.

userStories.title: Golden set leaked into few-shot exemplars — every exemplar eval number was suspect
userStories.description: Train/test contamination in the grading engine. Golden eval cases are grown from corrected human reviews (grading-eval.ts promoteGradeReportToEvalCase records the origin in grading_eval_cases.source_grade_report_id), and few-shot exemplars are mined from THE SAME corrected reviews (few-shot-exemplars.ts assembleExemplarSet) with no cross-exclusion. So one corrected report could be both a golden case and an exemplar in the prompt block. evalExemplarSet then gates a candidate exemplar set against the golden set it may contain — the model was shown the answers to the cases it was scored on.
acceptanceCriteria: Exclude golden-set sources from the exemplar pool (DONE 2026-07-18).
Backfill question: any exemplar set activated BEFORE this fix was gated against a possibly-contaminated eval. Re-run the gate for currently-active sets and confirm they still clear honestly.
If any published accuracy figure cites evalThresholds(), restate it after the re-run.
userStories.notes: [P1][Grading/Correctness] Found 2026-07-18 by the grading-engine deep dive; I VERIFIED it myself before acting (source_grade_report_id does exist on grading_eval_cases, and a grep for any exclusion in few-shot-exemplars.ts returned nothing). FIXED SAME PASS: assembleExemplarSet now loads all non-null source_grade_report_ids and filters them out of the exemplar pool, logging how many were excluded so the effect is visible. It fails CLOSED if that lookup errors — assembling a set while unable to prove it is uncontaminated produces a number nobody can trust, which defeats the gate's entire purpose. Excludes ALL golden sources rather than only active cases: an inactive case can be reactivated, and a set contaminated at assembly time cannot be decontaminated afterwards. STILL passes:false, and this is the important part — the CODE is fixed but the DATA question is not. Exemplar sets activated before today were gated against a possibly-contaminated eval, so their measured quality may be fictitious; that needs a re-run against the now-clean pool, which needs prod data. Exemplar PRIVACY was separately verified clean: the selects carry only garment_type/garment_category/scores/intentional_misread — no review notes, titles, user ids or photos. [2026-07-19 AC1 NOW GUARDED — AC2/AC3 STILL NEED PROD DATA] The AC1 fix from 2026-07-18 shipped with ZERO tests: nothing in src/tests referenced source_grade_report_id or contamination at all. A train/test contamination fix that is fixed but unguarded is one refactor away from returning, and its symptom is an eval number that looks BETTER than the truth — the failure mode nobody investigates. Extracted the train/test separation from the middle of assembleExemplarSet into a pure exported separateGoldenSources(), matching the repo idiom (planReversal / evaluateAlerts): the decision that keeps the eval gate honest should not be observable only through a Supabase call. Behaviour unchanged. 7 tests: golden report excluded; clean pool untouched; NULL source ids never match (source_grade_report_id is nullable for hand-authored cases — a null collapsing into a match would silently empty the pool); total overlap yields an EMPTY pool rather than falling back to contaminated candidates; duplicate golden rows counted once (several eval cases can share one source report, so excludedCount must describe candidates removed, not golden rows seen, or the log misreports contamination). Plus two source-level guards the pure function cannot cover: the lookup FAILS CLOSED, and the exclusion query is not narrowed by is_active/deleted_at — narrowing looks like a tidy-up and would quietly re-open the hole. Both negative-verified (injected .eq(is_active,true), and fail-closed -> fail-open; each caught by exactly its guard). UNCHANGED AND STILL BLOCKING: AC2 needs a re-run of the exemplar gate for currently-active sets against the now-clean pool — that is prod data, not code. AC3 is conditional on AC2. Any exemplar set activated before 2026-07-18 was gated against a possibly-contaminated eval, so its measured quality may be fictitious.

userStories.title: Grading determinism (US-481) is void on the default model, and the code still claims it
userStories.description: ai-config.ts:157-179 documents that grading ALWAYS uses a low temperature, defaulting to 0 (fully greedy decoding), because a certified score backs a public 'standardized' value prop. But gradingSamplingParams() returns output_config.effort — not temperature — for effort-based models, and the default grading model (DEFAULTS.model = claude-sonnet-5) is effort-based. So getGradingTemperature() is never called on the shipping path, GRADING_MAX_TEMPERATURE and the whole clamping apparatus are dead code, and grading runs at the model's own non-greedy decoding. A regrade of the same photos can return a different score with no explanation.
acceptanceCriteria: DECIDE the product position: is a regrade of identical photos allowed to return a different score? That is a trust question, not an engineering one.
If determinism is still the promise: add a self-consistency check (grade twice, compare, flag divergence) or pin a decoding mode that guarantees it.

If it is NOT the promise: correct the ai-config.ts comment block, which currently asserts a property the code does not have, and disclose run-to-run variance wherever the 'standardized grade' claim is made.
Either way the comment must stop describing temperature clamping as though it governs grading.
userStories.notes: [P1][Grading/Trust] Found 2026-07-18 by the grading-engine deep dive. I VERIFIED the mechanism myself: DEFAULTS.model is claude-sonnet-5 (ai-config.ts:12), modelUsesEffort() matches it (:189-192), and gradingSamplingParams() returns the effort branch with no temperature (:228-233). This is NOT a code bug — effort-based models do not accept temperature, so the US-1033 migration was a correct API fix. The defect is that it silently removed a DOCUMENTED GUARANTEE and nobody updated the guarantee. Code that claims a property it no longer has is the most dangerous state for a trust product, because everyone downstream reasons from the claim rather than the behaviour. I deliberately did not 'fix' it: the right answer is a product decision — restore determinism (costly, possibly not available on this model family) or stop promising it (cheap, but it changes what a certificate means). [2026-07-19 PARTIAL — AC3(a)+AC4 DONE, AC1/AC2/AC3(b) BLOCKED ON A PRODUCT DECISION] Verified the technical claim in full: getDefaultModel()=claude-sonnet-5 is effort-based, so gradingSamplingParams() returns output_config.effort and NO temperature; getGradingTemperature()/GRADING_MAX_TEMPERATURE are dead on the shipping path. Found a THIRD layer the story did not name: grading-reliability.ts implements the self-consistency math AC2 asks for, is pure and tested, but has ZERO non-test callers — the env-gated live-sampling job it describes was never built. So the determinism promise is unenforced at every level: no greedy decoding, no measurement, no gate. Done: both false comment blocks (ai-config.ts, grading-reliability.ts) now describe reality and name the open decision; new src/tests/grading-determinism_test.ts pins the actual behaviour (4 tests) so the claim cannot silently drift back. BLOCKED: AC1 is explicitly a trust/product call — is a regrade of identical photos allowed to return a different score? AC2 depends on that answer (wire grading-reliability.ts as a live self-consistency gate vs accept variance); AC3(b) public-copy disclosure depends on it too. NOTE: do NOT remedy by pinning a temperature — effort-based models 400 on it (US-1033).

userStories.title: 37 SEO/hydration tests and 11 money/cert integration tests never run in CI
userStories.description: Two distinct silent-skip classes. (a) STRUCTURAL: ci.yml orders steps Lint, Type-check, Test, Build — but three suites gate on existsSync(dist/index.html): prerender.test.ts:103 (10 tests), crawl-parity.test.ts:57 (1), responsive-images.test.ts:198 (26). dist/ is gitignored, so on a fresh runner it does not exist when tests run.
