acceptanceCriteria: Move the vitest step AFTER Build in ci.yml (or add a second post-build pass) so the dist-gated suites actually execute.
Stand up a job that provides the integration env vars, or delete those suites — a test that has never run is worse than no test, because it reads as coverage.
Apply the US-350 anti-skip pattern to both classes: make a missing fixture a hard CI failure rather than a silent skip.
userStories.notes: [P1][CI/Testing] Found 2026-07-18 by the test-suite deep dive. Same class as US-1998 (a gate that fails early hides every gate behind it) seen from the other side: a gate that SKIPS silently is indistinguishable from one that passes. The repo already solved this once — tenant-isolation_test.ts:90-107 carries an explicit 'must not SKIP in CI' guard wired to TENANT_ISOLATION_REQUIRED=1. The mechanism exists; it simply was never applied to these suites. Note the ordering fix is nearly free and would light up 37 tests immediately. | 2026-07-18 AC1 FIXED + AUDIT COUNT CORRECTED (agent loop). ⚠ THE NUMBER IN THIS STORY'S TITLE IS WRONG: the audit said 37 dist-gated tests; the real figure is 17. I measured it rather than trusting it — moved dist/ aside and ran the three suites: 34 passed / 17 SKIPPED (51 total). responsive-images.test.ts and crawl-parity.test.ts largely do NOT gate on dist the way the audit assumed; only prerender.test.ts's describe.skipIf block does. The FINDING is real and the fix is the same, but this is the fourth audit claim this session that was wrong in its specifics — the pattern is now consistent enough to treat every audit number as a hypothesis until measured. FIXED: ci.yml now runs Build BEFORE Test. That ordering is only safe because of the US-1998 `if: !cancelled()` rule — a failing build no longer skips the test step, so moving Build earlier cannot hide test results. prerender.test.ts's own comment already CLAIMED 'CI runs them after npm run build'; it did not, and now it does. Bonus: local and CI now measure the same thing. My local runs always had dist/ present, so I was running 17 tests CI never ran — coverage re-measured in the new state at 66.55/59.72/64.18/68.36 against floors 65/58/62/67, still clear. PUSHED (no migration dependency), unlike the rest of the stack. STILL passes:false on AC2/AC3: the 11 money/cert integration suites (ledger-consistency_test.ts above all — the credit-ledger balance invariant) still have NO CI job at all, and neither class carries the US-350 anti-skip guard that would make a missing fixture fail rather than skip. | 2026-07-19 AC1 VERIFIED ALREADY DONE; AC3 DONE for class (a); AC2 still needs a decision. AC1 is shipped — ci.yml now orders Build BEFORE 'Test (with coverage)', with the reorder explained in place and made safe by the if:!cancelled() rule (a failing build no longer prevents the test step, so moving Build earlier does not hide test results). Verified in the workflow, not assumed. AC3 IS THE DURABLE HALF AND IS WHAT I ADDED. AC1's fix is a STEP ORDER IN A YAML FILE: one reorder, or one build that stops emitting index.html, and all 37 SEO/hydration guards go back to skipping silently — with a skip and a pass looking identical in the CI summary, which is the entire failure mode. New src/test/dist-required.ts: requireDist() SKIPS locally (you have not necessarily built) but THROWS in CI. It throws at MODULE LOAD rather than inside a test, deliberately — a thrown suite is a loud red file, whereas a failing assertion inside a suite that 'ran 0 tests' is easy to scroll past. Wired into all three gated suites (prerender.test.ts, crawl-parity.test.ts, responsive-images.test.ts), replacing three copies of the same bare existsSync condition with one shared decision. Mirrors the pattern the repo already uses in tenant-isolation_test.ts (TENANT_ISOLATION_REQUIRED=1), which is cited by the story itself as the mechanism that solved this once. The DIST_TESTS_REQUIRED=0 escape hatch is opt-OUT rather than opt-in, because the failure being guarded against is precisely someone not thinking about it. NEGATIVE-VERIFIED IN BOTH DIRECTIONS, by actually moving dist/index.html aside: with CI=true the suite FAILS loudly naming US-2038 and the missing path; with CI unset it skips quietly as before; with CI=true plus DIST_TESTS_REQUIRED=0 it skips again. All three states confirmed by running them, not by reading the code. tsc also caught the now-unused existsSync import in responsive-images.test.ts, which is the tidy confirmation the old bare check is genuinely gone rather than merely bypassed. STILL OPEN — AC2, and it is a DECISION not a task: the 11 money/cert integration tests (credit-refund, ledger-consistency, ai-quota-concurrency, public-certificate, passport-claim) gate on TEST_SUPABASE_URL / TEST_LEDGER_USER_ID etc. and have no CI job at all. Either stand up a job with those env vars, or delete the suites — the story's own wording is right that a test which has never run is worse than no test, because it reads as coverage. I did not choose between them: standing up the job needs credentials I do not have, and deleting money-path tests is not a call to make unilaterally. Verified: web 2286 passed, tsc clean, lint 0 errors. [2026-07-19 AC3 NOW COMPLETE — both classes. AC2 STILL A DECISION] AC3 says apply the anti-skip pattern to BOTH classes; only class (a) (dist-gated) had it. Class (b) — the five money/cert integration suites — still printed SKIPPED and passed, and in a CI summary a skip and a pass are indistinguishable. Added src/tests/integration-required.ts (requireIntegrationFixtures) and wired all five: credit-refund (2 tests), ledger-consistency (1), ai-quota-concurrency (1), public-certificate (3), passport-claim (4) — 11 tests total, replacing five copies of the same bare warn with one shared decision. CRITICAL PROPERTY: behaviour today is byte-for-byte UNCHANGED. With no job and no flag the suites skip exactly as before, so this lands safely BEFORE AC2 is decided. It does not pre-empt AC2; it makes AC2 stick. Without it, the job AC2 asks for could be stood up with one env var typo'd and report green forever — the same defect one layer up. DELIBERATE INVERSION vs dist-required.ts: fixtures are opt-IN (INTEGRATION_TESTS_REQUIRED=1) whereas dist is opt-OUT. Every CI lane builds, so dist can default to required; most lanes legitimately cannot reach a database, and a guard that reddens every unrelated PR gets switched off — which is how anti-skip guards die. A BLANK env var counts as MISSING, not set: a CI secret that fails to resolve expands to "" rather than being absent, and treating that as configured is exactly how a job reports green while asserting nothing. Tested. NEGATIVE-VERIFIED END TO END by running both states, not by reading: no flag -> ledger-consistency skips quietly (1 ignored); INTEGRATION_TESTS_REQUIRED=1 with fixtures absent -> loud module-load failure naming the suite and all three missing vars. 5 helper tests + 4341 edge tests green. STILL OPEN — AC2 ONLY, and unchanged as a decision: stand up a CI job providing TEST_SUPABASE_URL / TEST_SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY / TEST_LEDGER_USER_ID / TEST_CREDIT_USER_ID / TEST_QUOTA_USER_ID / TEST_SUPABASE_ANON_KEY / TEST_PUBLIC_CERTIFICATE_ID / TEST_EDGE_BASE_URL / TEST_PASSPORT_GARMENT_ID and set INTEGRATION_TESTS_REQUIRED=1 — or delete the suites. Needs credentials I do not have; deleting money-path tests is not a unilateral call. ledger-consistency asserts the credit-ledger balance invariant and has still never run in CI. | 2026-07-19 A THIRD SILENT-SKIP CLASS, FOUND BY ACCIDENT AND FIXED. This story enumerated two classes (dist-gated suites ordered before Build; integration suites with no CI job). There was a third it did not name: suites CI NEVER INVOKED AT ALL because they run under a different vitest config or a bare node script. scripts/*.test.mjs (~190 tests: prd-lint, prd-digest, doc-refs, submit-indexnow, vault tooling) run under vitest.scripts.config.mjs, while ci.yml only ran `npm run test:coverage`, whose config includes src/** only. And scripts/test-extensions.mjs (15 zero-dep suites over the three MV3 extensions) appeared in ZERO workflow files. Both ran solely via `npm run verify`, i.e. the local pre-push hook — which a --no-verify push skips entirely. So the hook was STRICTER than the pipeline it claims to mirror, and CLAUDE.md calls verify 'CI parity'. NOT HYPOTHETICAL, and this is how I found it: scripts/prd-lint.test.mjs went RED on 2026-07-18 when the learnings file moved into the vault (US-2061) and the lint message followed but the test's case-sensitive assertion did not. I verified it was red AT that commit (1 failed | 182 passed) and that 15 further commits touched scripts/ before I found it by hand today. Exactly this story's thesis — a suite that reads as coverage while never executing. WORSE, AND THE REASON I FIXED IT IMMEDIATELY RATHER THAN FILING IT: two guards I wrote THIS SESSION live in the extension suite — the legacy-unified selector-parity guard (US-2020, written because a hand-sync failure had already shipped a broken Poshmark delist) and the Firefox version-floor guard (US-1881 follow-up, written because a missing strict_min_version had already shipped). Both were written against real incidents and NEITHER COULD HAVE FAILED THE BUILD. Added four steps to ci.yml — Test (scripts), Extension tests, PRD lint, Doc path refs — closing the verify/CI parity gap. All four verified to exit 0 today, so this does not redden CI on a pre-existing failure, and `npm run test:scripts` verified to exit 1 on a planted failure so the step can actually fail. AC1/AC3 remain as previously recorded; AC2 (integration env vars) still needs credentials. | 2026-07-19 (related, not this story) Continued the sweep for DOCUMENTED RULES WITH NO ENFORCEMENT that this story's thesis implies. Two more closed today: US-1552's .or()-on-mutation ban (CLAUDE.md states outright that CI cannot catch it, since the local PostgREST accepts what prod rejects) and US-276's private-bucket rule (submission-images never via getPublicUrl; signed-URL TTL <= 900s). Both were clean at time of writing, so both are ratchets rather than repairs. THE TTL HALF IS THE ONE WORTH NOTING: a signed URL above the cap WORKS PERFECTLY — nothing fails, no test reddens, no user complains, and the only consequence is that a leaked link outlives policy. That is structurally invisible to every runtime test, which is the same category as .or() on a mutation and the same category this story is about. | 2026-07-19 (cont.) THE ENFORCEMENT SWEEP FOUND AN ACTUAL DEFECT, not just a missing guard. Checked whether US-276's upload pipeline is APPLIED as well as available — upload-validation_test.ts proves the validator works, nothing proved anyone calls it. Enumerated all 20 storage.upload() sites: 11 validate, 9 do not. Read all 9; eight are legitimately server-generated or derived (rendered overlays, OG cards, a JSON archive, thumbnails from already-validated originals). THE NINTH WAS REAL: flipdesk-disclosure.ts accepted a client-supplied base64 PNG data URL, checked ONLY the declared `data:image/png;base64,` prefix — client-asserted MIME, which is precisely what CLAUDE.md says not to trust — and uploaded it to item-photos, the PUBLIC bucket, with no magic-byte sniff and no EXIF strip. Demonstrated the hole rather than asserting it: an SVG behind that prefix passes the regex, and validateImageUpload rejects it as 'SVG images are not allowed' precisely because SVG is script-bearing and the bucket is world-readable. Fixed with the established pattern (validate allow:['png'] then strip). ALSO GUARDED THE HEIC INVARIANT, whose rationale is easy to misread as a compatibility nit: HEIC EXIF lives in an ISOBMFF meta box the dependency-free stripper cannot parse, and HEIC embeds GPS like JPEG, so an admitted HEIC would store LIVE COORDINATES of where the photo was taken. That guarantee was held up by 15 hand-written allow: lists plus a runtime throw — the runtime throw fires in prod on a real user's photo; the guard fires at build time on the commit. I ALSO NEARLY FILED A FALSE FINDING: I suspected the grading path copying item-photos into the private bucket could smuggle HEIC past the private allowlist, and checked instead of reporting — zero upload paths admit HEIC, so item-photos cannot contain it and the copy is safe. ⚠ MOST IMPORTANT: MY OWN GUARD SHIPPED WITH A HOLE AND I CAUGHT IT ONLY BY PLANTING THE DEFECT. v1 looked back a fixed 3000 chars for the string 'validateImageUpload' — which the IMPORT LINE and a DIFFERENT HANDLER both satisfy, so deleting the real validation left it green. That is the THIRD time this session a source guard matched context rather than the property under test (US-2103 hand-listed builders, US-2104 import line). Rescoped to the enclosing function and to a CALL with its paren, which an import cannot satisfy; the re-planted defect now fails naming flipdesk-disclosure.ts:269. Verified: 4459 edge tests, deno check + lint clean. | 2026-07-19 (cont.) RAN THE FULL `npm run verify` ACROSS BOTH SESSIONS' WORK — nobody had, and it was RED. Two failures, both mine, both invisible to the way I had been checking. (1) `deno lint` failed on a prefer-const in my own private-bucket guard. I had been running `deno lint | tail -1`, which prints 'Checked N files' and HIDES the error block above it — I read the last line and called it clean, repeatedly. (2) The web vitest lane failed because THE OTHER SESSION HAD INDEPENDENTLY WRITTEN THE SAME US-1552 GUARD (src/lib/__tests__/no-or-on-mutations.test.ts, US-2129) and its repo-wide scan flagged MY guard's deliberate bad-code FIXTURES as real violations. Two guards for one rule is the duplication this repo keeps paying for, so I consolidated to one rather than adding an exclusion: DELETED MINE (theirs scans the whole repo and runs in the main web CI job; mine was edge-only) and PORTED MY CHAIN WALKER INTO THEIRS, because theirs sliced to the first semicolon and therefore missed `.update({ note: "a; b" }).or(...)` — a false NEGATIVE on the exact bug it exists to catch. THE PORT IMMEDIATELY PRODUCED A FALSE POSITIVE AND I ALMOST SHIPPED IT: the walker flagged flipdesk-ebay.ts:6058, a correct .update().eq(). Cause worth remembering — the comment above it contains "didn't", and the walker treated that apostrophe as an opening string delimiter that never closed, swallowing the rest of the file until it found an unrelated .or(). It now skips // and /* */ comments BEFORE string handling. A false positive is how a guard gets disabled, so that mattered more than the false negative I set out to fix. Both directions re-verified by planting: a real .or() on a mutation, and the semicolon-in-string variant the original missed. Net: one guard, broader scope than mine, better detection than theirs. Verified: 2472 web + 4457 edge tests, deno lint/check clean. | 2026-07-19 ⚠ CORRECTION TO THE ENTRY ABOVE — I MISREPORTED WHY THAT GUARD COLLIDED, AND THE TRUTH IS WORSE. I described the US-1552 .or() guard as something the other session had 'independently written', i.e. a concurrent duplicate. It was not concurrent. src/lib/__tests__/no-or-on-mutations.test.ts was added on 2026-07-18 by US-2081/2082, was already on origin/main before this session started, and US-2129 had since hardened it. So it was PRE-EXISTING and I simply failed to find it. My commit for that work (22c69623) states 'until now the rule lived solely as a sentence in CLAUDE.md — read by humans at session start and by nothing at build time'. That sentence is FALSE and should not be trusted by anyone reading the history. ROOT CAUSE, and it is embarrassing given the subject: before writing the guard I searched `grep -rln "US-1552" services/edge-functions/src/tests/ scripts/` — two directories, NEITHER of which is where the guard lived. A repo-wide grep finds it instantly (verified after the fact: it returns src/lib/__tests__/no-or-on-mutations.test.ts as the second hit). I scoped a search to where I ASSUMED the answer would be and read the empty result as proof of absence — which is precisely the failure mode of guards-that-cannot-fail shape 8, applied to my own research rather than to a test. The conclusion 'no guard exists' was an artifact of the search, not a fact about the repo. NET OUTCOME IS STILL POSITIVE and the consolidation stands: the surviving guard now has the chain walker (closing a false negative on a semicolon inside a string argument) plus comment-skipping (closing a false positive I introduced), and there is one guard rather than two. But the framing was wrong, so: BEFORE ADDING ANY GUARD, GREP THE WHOLE REPO FOR THE RULE ID, NOT THE DIRECTORY YOU EXPECT IT IN.

userStories.title: admin/disputes.tsx rounded the weighted overall to 0.5 while the server stored 0.1

userStories.title: iOS: bulk photo import is strictly serial though a bounded-concurrency helper already exists
userStories.description: Both PHPicker import paths — AutoListerReviewModel.swift:218-243 and PhotoIntakeView.swift:907-923 — are plain serial for loops awaiting per photo: result.loadImage() (I/O; for iCloud-backed photos a NETWORK round trip each), then PhotoCompressor.compressOffMain (CPU), then a detached DHash.compute (CPU, :238-240). Meanwhile PhotoCompressor.compressBatch(_:maxConcurrent:) (PhotoCompressor.swift:64-91) exists for exactly this — bounded concurrency, per-item autoreleasepool, order-preserving — and a grep of the whole ios/ tree shows its ONLY caller is Inventory/PhotosDropHandler.swift:20. Neither high-volume import path uses it.
acceptanceCriteria: Wrap the whole per-photo unit (load + compress + dHash) in the chunked withTaskGroup shape already used correctly three times in this codebase: PhotoCompressor.compressBatch, DisclosureStore.renderAll (Disclosure/DisclosureStore.swift:88-115) and ReconciliationService (:215-242).

Keep concurrency modest (3-4) so only a few full-resolution UIImages are resident — that memory property is why compressBatch was written, and parallelising without it trades a latency win for a jetsam risk.
Preserve input order via the enumerate-and-sort approach at DisclosureStore.swift:106.
userStories.notes:
[P2][iOS/Performance] Found 2026-07-18 by the iOS audit. The dominant cost is loadImage(), not compression: for iCloud-backed photos that is a serialized network fetch per photo, so a 200-photo import is 200 sequential round trips. Symptom: bulk import sits on the spinner for minutes rather than tens of seconds when photos are not local, and it widens the window for the 'still downloading from iCloud' partial-failure path the code already anticipates (:255-259). NOT FIXED HERE — Swift is unbuildable on Windows.

VERIFIED 2026-07-18 — REAL, still open, deliberately NOT fixed blind.

Confirmed at PhotoIntakeView.ingestLibraryPicks (:907): a plain `for result in results` loop awaiting result.loadImage() then compressOffMain per item. Strictly serial, so 200 iCloud-backed photos are 200 sequential network round trips.

Refinement to the story premise: the existing helper CANNOT be applied directly. PhotoCompressor.compressBatch takes [UIImage] — images already in memory — while the bottleneck is loadImage() upstream of it. What compressBatch does provide is the exact PATTERN to copy: a windowed `withTaskGroup(of: (Int, T).self)` writing into a pre-sized results array, which preserves picker order (the loop comment notes order matters for the tray) and bounds residency.

DESIGN CONSTRAINT worth recording, because the obvious implementation is wrong: do NOT load all images first and then call compressBatch. compressBatch own header explains why — it keeps only a few full-resolution UIImages resident so a large drop does not spike memory into a jetsam kill. Loading 200 full-res UIImages up front reintroduces exactly that risk. The correct shape is ONE windowed TaskGroup where each task does loadImage + compress together, so at most maxConcurrent full-res images exist at any moment.

Why not fixed here: this is ~25 lines of NEW concurrent Swift on the bulk-import path, with ordering and memory-residency invariants, and it cannot be compiled or tested on this Windows checkout. That is a different risk class from the one-word LazyHStack change — needs a macOS session.

Highest-value GEO item after the empty-report fix. | 2026-07-19 AC4+AC5 DONE (the code half); AC1/AC2/AC3 remain BUSINESS ACTIONS — the profiles do not exist, and the code is already correct in emitting nothing rather than placeholders, so there is nothing to write until someone creates accounts they will actually maintain. AC5 (certificate Products orphaned) got the same treatment for the same reason: US-425 documented the cert Review author as deliberately inline because the cert page emits only Product + Breadcrumb, and that reasoning still holds — so the node keeps its name/url AND gains @id: ORG_ID. THE TEST IS THE PART WORTH READING: the first version listed five builders by hand, and when I reintroduced an anonymous node to check it, IT PASSED — none of the five happened to contain a fixed site. Rewrote it to DERIVE its coverage from every zero-arg *JsonLd export plus every FLIPDESK_LANDINGS entry (53 assertions), so a new builder is covered the day it is added. userStories.notes: [P2][Content] Found 2026-07-18 by the SEO/marketing deep-dive audit. GATED: the domain is new and pSEO volume is already an indexability risk (vault/40-growth/seo-indexability.md) — do not start until the GSC Page-indexing diagnosis (US-2095) is read. Publishing the four existing drafts is safe to do immediately; turning on AUTO-publish at volume is the part that must wait. Prereqs overlap US-1566 (crons/SES) — coordinate. | 2026-07-19 AC3 DONE; AC1/AC2/AC4/AC5 UNTOUCHED and correctly gated (they need the GSC diagnosis US-2095, Coolify crons and a pacing decision — ops actions, not code). AC3 was the one piece that is a pure correctness bug and is independent of the rollout gate, so it was safe to fix while the engine stays cold. THE BUG, confirmed by reading the path rather than trusting the description: with every make_webhook_social* unset — the current prod state — dispatchContentWebhook returns early with attempts:0 and writes NO content_webhook_log row and NO dead letter, while the route had already flipped the row to status='published'. Terminal state, no record, nothing to retry: the post is silently lost and the engine reports success. I ALSO FOUND THE SAME HOLE IN THE SCHEDULER TICK (content-scheduler.ts), which the story does not mention and which is strictly worse — it is unattended, so one tick drains the ENTIRE scheduled queue into 'published' with nothing sent. Fixing only the manual route would have left the automated path to do the damage at volume. DELIBERATELY DID NOT IMPLEMENT AC3 AS WRITTEN. The AC says do not mark published 'when the webhook is unset OR the POST failed'. The second half would REVERSE A SOUND EXISTING DECISION: a configured webhook that fails is logged, dead-lettered and replayable via POST /webhooks/:logId/retry, so nothing is lost and rolling back would break the replay workflow. The two cases only look alike — one is recoverable and recorded, the other is neither. So the guard checks CONFIGURATION, not DELIVERY. Implemented as a PRE-FLIGHT check rather than a post-hoc rollback, which avoids reordering publish-before-fanout and means there is never a published row to un-publish. Manual route returns 422 with a stable code (social_webhook_unconfigured); the scheduler leaves posts 'scheduled' and logs a warning naming the count — deferred, not dropped, and it explicitly does not rewrite scheduled_for, or a misconfiguration would silently push the backlog into the future. hasAnySocialWebhookConfigured FAILS OPEN on a settings read error: the failure being fixed is a confident false success, not a blocked publish, and an unreachable settings row is not evidence of misconfiguration. 6 tests, including empty-string-is-not-a-destination (a blank settings value reading as configured is the same class as a CI secret that fails to resolve and reports green) and legacy long/short still counting as configured. NEGATIVE-VERIFICATION CAUGHT A FLAW IN MY OWN TEST, worth recording: removing the scheduler guard left the test GREEN, because it searched for the bare identifier and matched the surviving IMPORT line at the top of the file, which trivially satisfies every 'appears before the loop' assertion. Retargeted at the call expression; the removal now reddens it. A guard test that a deleted guard passes is worse than no test — same lesson as the US-2103 hand-listed builder sweep earlier this session. Verified: 4437 edge tests pass, deno check + lint clean.

userStories.title: The grading standard has qualitative criteria but no measurable tolerances
userStories.description: PSA is citable because its standard is measurable: '55/45 front, 75/25 reverse'. GradeThread's is 'noticeable pilling, light fading' — good rubric, not a citable spec. Confirmed: no tolerance or measurement language anywhere in grading-scale.ts or grade-standard.ts. Relatedly, /grading/methodology is the weakest page relative to its promise: no named base model, no eval numbers, and the confidence threshold is described only as 'below our threshold' — it is 0.75 and it is documented in CLAUDE.md.
acceptanceCriteria: Add measurable tolerances where the factor genuinely admits them (pilling density, fade delta-E, hole/tear dimensions in mm, seam separation length, stain area).
State the 0.75 human-review confidence threshold explicitly on /grading/methodology.
State what can be said about the model and evaluation without leaking prompt IP.
Render tier data and flaw->factor->impact as real <table> elements — /condition-grading currently uses div cards, and tables are the structure most often lifted verbatim into LLM answers.
Coordinate with the grading-engine skill contract before changing any published criterion.
userStories.notes: [P2][GEO/Authority] Found 2026-07-18 by the SEO/marketing deep-dive audit. This is the explicit PSA-playbook gap in the strategy doc's own mapping table, and it is the difference between 'a rubric' and 'the standard'. Adds no new URLs. [2026-07-19 PARTIAL — AC2+AC4 DONE, AC1 SUBSTANTIALLY DONE, AC3+AC5 OPEN] KEY FINDING: the premise was half wrong. The story says no tolerance language exists anywhere; true of grading-scale.ts/grade-standard.ts, but defect-weighting.ts has carried REAL measurable data since US-1028 — physical size buckets in mm (pinhole <3mm, small 3-13mm, medium 13-50mm, large >50mm), SEVERITY_MULT, and a full FACTOR_ROUTING defect->factor table. We were not missing the measurable standard, we were failing to PUBLISH it. Nothing had to be invented. Done: AC2 the 0.75 review threshold is stated explicitly on /grading/methodology via a guarded constant (grading-threshold-parity.test.ts fails if it diverges from the edge fallback); AC4 tier data is now a real <table> with scope/caption, and three new spec tables render the mm tolerances, severity multipliers and flaw->factor routing. New src/lib/grading-standard.ts mirrors the engine (frontend cannot import from services/edge-functions) and grading-standard-parity.test.ts guards every mirrored value, including that unknown size stays <= small so missing data never inflates a penalty. DELIBERATE OMISSION: BASE_WEIGHT (exact score-points penalty per defect type) is NOT published. Publishing which factor a flaw hits makes the standard auditable; publishing the exact penalty makes it gameable — a seller who knows the arithmetic photographs to minimise it. A test asserts it stays out. Reversing that is a product call. STILL OPEN: AC1 residue — pilling density and fade delta-E have NO engine equivalent and were deliberately not invented; adding them means defining new measurement in the engine first. AC3 (name the base model + eval numbers without leaking prompt IP) is unstarted and overlaps the US-2035 determinism decision. AC5 requires grading-engine skill/vault coordination since this now publishes engine criteria. | 2026-07-19 AC5 DONE. AC5 read like a process footnote and is actually the load-bearing one: publishing engine criteria CHANGED WHAT A CHANGE TO THEM MEANS, and nothing recorded that. SIZE_BUCKETS, SEVERITY_MULT and FACTOR_ROUTING went public on /condition-grading, but defect-weighting.ts — the file someone actually opens to tune grading — said nothing about it, and neither did the vault. So the natural next edit is a private calibration tweak that silently makes a published spec wrong. Fixed at the point of edit AND in the contract: a header warning on defect-weighting.ts naming exactly which three tables are mirrored and why that matters (the page exists to be cited and lifted verbatim into LLM answers, so a stale mirror is a precise, checkable, WRONG claim — worse than the adjectives it replaced), plus a new 'Published criteria' section in vault/20-domain/grading-scale-and-weights.md with defect-weighting.ts and grading-standard.ts added to code_refs so the CI drift guard now watches them. THE NON-OBVIOUS FACT, and I VERIFIED IT RATHER THAN ASSUMING: the parity guard lives in the WEB project, so `deno test` alone does NOT catch an engine-side change. Proved it by moving SEVERITY_MULT.minor 0.5 -> 0.6 with the mirror untouched — the edge suite passed 18/18 completely happily while the web guard failed on 'severity multipliers match SEVERITY_MULT'. An engine developer running the obvious local suite would have shipped it. That is now called out in both the source warning and the note, with the instruction to run npm run verify. Also carried the BASE_WEIGHT omission into both places as a PRODUCT TRADE-OFF rather than an unfinished edge — auditable vs gameable — because 'the published standard is missing the penalties' reads like a completeness bug to anyone who has not seen the argument. STILL OPEN: AC1 residue (pilling density, fade delta-E have no engine equivalent; adding them means defining new measurement in the engine first, not writing prose) and AC3 (naming the base model + eval numbers), which remains blocked behind the US-2035 determinism product decision. userStories.title: Viral-loop attribution leaks and a blank certificate OG fallback
userStories.description: The certificate share loop is the designated organic acquisition flywheel, and it leaks at three points: buyer-to-buyer re-shares carry no ref= because the code gates on !!user (src/components/.../cert-share-actions.tsx:54), so the highest-reach shares are unattributed; the SSR cert CTA drops attribution entirely (functions/cert/[id].ts:249); and the cert OG image falls back to a transparent 1x1 PNG on edge failure (functions/og/cert/[id].ts:24), cached 300s — a blank link preview, which is worse for CTR than a branded fallback.
acceptanceCriteria: Attach a referral/attribution parameter to every cert share path, including anonymous re-shares.
Preserve attribution through the SSR CTA.
Replace the 1x1 transparent fallback with a branded static OG image.
Mount the PWA install prompt somewhere with real install intent — it is currently only on flipdesk/intake.tsx:489 and snap.tsx:80, not the dashboard or landing.
userStories.notes: [P2][Growth] Found 2026-07-18 by the SEO/marketing deep-dive audit. Depends on US-1945 (cert pages 404 in prod) being fixed first — the loop is dead until then. | 2026-07-19 AC1+AC3 DONE; AC2 DELIBERATELY NOT DONE (argued below); AC4 untouched. First, the stated DEPENDENCY IS STALE: US-1945 says cert pages 404 in prod, but its own latest note records the certificate it names still returning HTTP 200 live — what is actually missing is the homepage sample-cert link (an unset Pages env var). Cert pages resolve, so the share loop is not dead and this was workable. AC1: attribution was built as one refSuffix that appeared ONLY when the viewer had a referral code, which coupled two different things. ref= is a CLAIM ON A CREDIT and needs someone to credit; utm_* is a DESCRIPTION OF A PATH and is true regardless. Split them: every share now carries utm_source/medium/campaign (cert_referral vs cert_organic, so the two halves of the loop can be measured separately) plus per-channel utm_content, while ref= still appears only for a sharer who actually has a code. EXPLICITLY DID NOT make anonymous re-shares inherit the ref the visitor arrived with — that is the tempting version of this fix and it would credit a seller for a stranger's audience, inventing an earning event while looking like closing an attribution gap. Pinned by a test that fails if an anonymous share ever carries a ref. AC3: the 1x1 transparent fallback is not just the cert — it is the SAME defect in all five og/* endpoints (cert, blog, verified, grade-check, social/card), so I fixed the class via a shared brandedFallbackResponse() that streams the existing static /og-image.png and drops to the pixel only if that is also unreachable. Deliberately NOT applied to badge/* and slab/*: those have their own dimensions, and an invisible badge degrades better than a wrong-shaped brand card stretched into a badge slot. Fallback TTL stays 300s against the real card's 24h, because this response means upstream was unavailable — caching a generic card for a day at a scraper we cannot purge would outlast the outage and permanently mis-image every share created in that window. Added an X-GT-Fallback header since a degraded card and a real one are otherwise both just a 200 with PNG bytes. AC2 IS THE INTERESTING ONE AND I DID NOT DO IT, because doing it as written is a correctness bug: the cert SSR response is SHARED-EDGE-CACHED on origin+pathname with the query string DROPPED (withEdgeCache in blog-render.ts), so varying the CTA href by the visitor's ?ref= would cache the first arriver's referral code and serve it to every later visitor of that certificate — one seller silently credited for everyone else's traffic, which is strictly worse than the leak. And there is almost nothing to preserve: /cert/:id renders under RootLayout, which calls captureAffiliateRef() on mount, so a JS-enabled visitor banks the ref before they can click the link; the gap is no-JS agents, which are overwhelmingly crawlers, and a crawler does not sign up. Reasoning left as a comment at the CTA so the next person does not 'fix' it into cache poisoning. This is the third audit claim this session that did not survive verification (cf. US-2030, US-2020). AC4 (PWA install prompt placement) not started — it is a UX placement decision, not a defect. Verified: 2472 web tests pass, tsc -b + functions tsconfig clean, negative-verified both the pre-fix coupling and the borrow-a-ref variant. | 2026-07-22 AC4 DONE (agent loop). The prior note left AC4 as an untaken UX placement decision, but the AC itself names the surfaces ('not the dashboard or landing'), so this is an implementation, not a fresh decision: mounted <PwaInstallBanner variant="general"/> on src/pages/dashboard.tsx (right under the PageHeader). The banner is inert unless the browser fires beforeinstallprompt AND the user has not dismissed it, and it shares ONE dismiss key across all mounts (intake/snap/dashboard), so adding a third surface never nags — it just reaches an engaged, returning user (the highest real install intent) instead of only the FlipDesk-intake/Snap paths. general variant copy is grades/certificates-oriented, correct for the consumer dashboard. Verified: tsc -b + eslint clean. STILL passes:false on AC2 ALONE, which is a documented CORRECTNESS refusal, not an oversight: the cert SSR response is shared-edge-cached on origin+pathname with the query string dropped (withEdgeCache), so varying the CTA href by the visitor ?ref= would cache the first arriver's referral code and serve it to everyone — AC2 as written is a cache-poisoning bug. Closing it needs a non-query-string mechanism (e.g. client-side capture after navigation), which is genuine remaining work. AC1 (split utm_* channel vs ref= credit, incl. anonymous shares) + AC3 (shared brandedFallbackResponse across all og/* endpoints) were already done. | Done 2026-07-30 (54f3bece). AC2 was the last open criterion and the prior refusal was half wrong. THE CACHE ARGUMENT WAS RIGHT and is preserved: the SSR cert response is shared-edge-cached on origin+pathname with the query string dropped (withEdgeCache, blog-render.ts), so rendering the visitor ?ref= into the CTA href would cache the first arriver code and credit one seller for everyone else traffic. Nothing does that now and the warning comment in functions/cert/[id].ts stays. THE SECOND CLAIM WAS FALSE and it was the reason the story stalled: the note said '/cert/:id renders under RootLayout, which calls captureAffiliateRef() on mount, so a JS-enabled visitor has already banked the ref' and concluded the exposure was limited to no-JS crawlers. VERIFIED FALSE by reading the renderer -- renderLayout emits no #root and no module script, and functions/_shared/security-headers.ts:14 states outright 'These pages are standalone (they do NOT mount the SPA)'. RootLayout runs only when the SPA is already loaded and routes to /cert/:id client-side, which is not what happens when someone opens a shared certificate link. So zero capture code ran for every visitor arriving through the share loop -- the whole flywheel, not an edge case. FIX: new functions/_shared/affiliate-capture.ts exports affiliateCaptureSnippet(nonce), a nonce-stamped inline script wired into renderLayout (NOT into the cert Function -- a shared link can carry a ref to any standalone SSR surface, so this is the same fix-the-class move AC3 made with brandedFallbackResponse). It reads ?ref= off the visitor OWN URL at runtime and writes {code,ts} to localStorage under gt_affiliate_ref, the exact key+shape readStored()/redeemStoredAffiliateRef() parse. The emitted bytes are identical for every visitor, so the response stays safe to shared-cache -- that is the property that makes this a fix rather than the cache-poisoning bug the old note feared. Validation is byte-for-byte identical to captureAffiliateRef (trim/uppercase/reject empty or >32) on purpose: a stricter SSR rule would mean a code that attributes on an SPA landing and silently does not on an SSR one. Returns '' without a nonce rather than emitting a script the CSP would silently block. CLICK PING DELIBERATELY NOT SENT FROM THE SSR PAGE: it is a cross-origin POST and the SSR CSP connect-src does not include the edge API; widening the CSP on the most XSS-sensitive surface in the repo to deliver telemetry is the wrong trade. Instead the payload is parked as pendingClick and sent by the new flushPendingAffiliateClick() (src/lib/affiliate.ts) from the next SPA load, wired in src/layouts/root-layout.tsx. It carries the ORIGINATING path+source, so a cert click does not report as a homepage hit, and it clears the marker BEFORE the request so a failed ping is dropped rather than re-sent on every later page (an affiliate click count that inflates while the visitor browses is worse than one missed click). The credit survives the flush -- only the marker is removed. Verified: 15 new tests in src/test/cert-ssr-attribution-capture.test.ts covering the cache-safety negative (no referral code in the rendered bytes, two renders byte-identical), the storage-shape contract across the SSR/SPA boundary executed in jsdom, the length-rule parity, single-shot flush, and TTL expiry. NEGATIVE-VERIFIED by planting both defects: dropping affiliateCaptureSnippet from renderLayout reddens 1 test, and forgetting to clear the pendingClick marker reddens 2. Full checks: tsc --noEmit clean, tsc -p tsconfig.functions.json clean, eslint 0 errors, npm test 225 files/2836 tests pass, npm run build green. AC1/AC3/AC4 were already done in earlier passes.

userStories.title: No product/pricing/UI A/B testing — PostHog flags are never read client-side
userStories.description: There is a sophisticated server-side flag engine with deterministic FNV-1a bucketing, rollout percentages and plan targeting (lib/feature-flags.ts:114-166), plus four experiment engines (lib/experiments-governor.ts:19) — but they cover email subject lines, drip timing and AI prompts only. PostHog is initialized yet only capture() is ever called (src/lib/analytics.ts:237-239); feature flags are never read, there is no client useFeatureFlag hook and no exposure event. So paywall copy, pricing presentation and onboarding cannot currently be tested. All the primitives exist — this is a connector, not a framework build.
acceptanceCriteria: Add a client useFeatureFlag hook backed by PostHog, with an exposure event so results are analyzable.
Respect the existing consent gating — no flag evaluation before consent.
Prove it with one real experiment on a conversion surface (paywall copy or pricing layout).
Document how server-side flags and client-side experiments relate, so the two systems do not drift.
userStories.notes: [P2][Growth/Experimentation] Found 2026-07-18 by the SEO/marketing deep-dive audit. Pairs with US-2101 (UTM capture) — together they make conversion work measurable rather than anecdotal. | 2026-07-19 AC1+AC2+AC4 DONE; AC3 (one real experiment) DELIBERATELY LEFT OPEN. The connector exists: src/lib/client-experiments.ts (logic, testable without React) + src/hooks/use-feature-flag.ts (subscription plumbing), returning {variant, ready}. The story called it a connector not a framework and that was right — this layer does NO bucketing, rollout or targeting, because PostHog already does all three. THREE INTEGRITY PROPERTIES, each of which is the difference between an experiment that reports a number and one whose number is true. (1) CONSENT IS STRUCTURAL, NOT CHECKED: flags are read off window.posthog, which analytics.ts only creates after opt-in, so there is no code path that can bucket an unconsented visitor — nothing exists to ask. AC2 is satisfied by construction rather than by a guard someone can forget. (2) NO MID-SESSION FLIPS: a resolved variant is LOCKED for the page session. PostHog re-delivers flags on identify and on payload refresh, and a paywall whose copy changes mid-read gives you a visitor who saw BOTH arms and belongs to neither. (3) EXPOSURE IS AN EVENT, NOT AN EVALUATION: experiment_exposed fires once per flag per session and only when the caller says the variant was actually SHOWN — the hook takes an `exposed` argument for surfaces that mount before they are visible. Analysing on $feature_flag_called (which fires when code merely ASKS) is the standard way a real effect gets diluted into a tie. THE SUBTLEST DECISION: undefined from getFeatureFlag is kept SEPARABLE from an actual control rather than collapsed into it. They look identical — both render control — but collapsing them counts every visitor into the control arm during the flag-load window, which makes a winning experiment read as a tie. That is why the return is {variant, ready} and not just a string. 13 tests. NEGATIVE-VERIFIED all three properties by simulating the careless edit: dropping the lock reddens 2, dropping the exposure resolution-guard reddens 1, collapsing undefined into control reddens 3; restoring returns to green. AC4 DONE as vault/40-growth/experimentation.md (contract) — and writing it surfaced a REAL FINDING the story did not anticipate: the Experiments Governor (US-1609) has adapters for the four server-side engines and NONE for client-side, so a paywall test is invisible to its interference detection and could run against the same conversion metric as a drip test with both reads looking clean. Recorded as a warning callout with the manual check to do meanwhile. Also noted: the consent category model has no vault note, which is a gap. AC3 NOT DONE ON PURPOSE: there is no web paywall component (paywall is iOS/Android), so the named surface is the pricing page, and choosing what to test there means authoring alternative pricing copy/layout — a product and design decision, not a code one. The mechanism is ready and wiring a chosen variant is now a small edit. Verified: 2462 web tests pass, tsc -b clean, vault:lint clean (3 drift warnings pre-existing from earlier commits today, not from this work).

userStories.title: Image sitemap covers 8 of 213 routes via a hand-synced list; CF Transformations still off
userStories.description: functions/_shared/sitemap.ts:379-441 hardcodes 8 marketing images with a 'KEEP IN SYNC with ROUTE_OG_IMAGES' comment (:378) and no CI guard — Pages Functions cannot import from src/, and unlike llms.txt (which solved the identical cross-boundary problem by consuming the build-emitted dist/seo-manifest.json) this one was left manual. Separately, VITE_CF_IMAGE_RESIZING=false in .env.production (verified, :39) gates the entire srcset in responsive-image.tsx:32-33, so production ships full-size originals with no srcset/sizes on every public image.
acceptanceCriteria: Generate MARKETING_IMAGES from dist/seo-manifest.json, mirroring the llms.txt approach, or add a CI guard on the sync.
Enable Cloudflare Transformations on the zone, then flip VITE_CF_IMAGE_RESIZING — in that order.
Do not flip the flag first: responsive-image.tsx:27-31 documents that a failed srcset candidate does not fall back to src, so enabling it before the zone feature renders every image broken.
userStories.notes: [P3][SEO/Perf] Found 2026-07-18 by the SEO/marketing deep-dive audit. width/height are already emitted so CLS is protected; the unrealized win is bytes/LCP. Blocked on a Cloudflare dashboard toggle, not code. | 2026-07-19 AC1 DONE; AC2/AC3 remain BLOCKED on a Cloudflare dashboard toggle (not code). The image sitemap no longer hand-syncs: vite.config.ts seoManifestPlugin emits a per-route `image` {file,alt} from ROUTE_OG_IMAGES into dist/seo-manifest.json, and functions/_shared/sitemap.ts marketingImageUrls derives from it — the same cross-boundary pattern llms.txt already used, which is what the story asked for. Verified parity: the derived set is EXACTLY the 8 the constant hardcoded, so this is a sourcing change with zero output diff today, and a new share card now arrives with no second edit. TWO JUDGEMENT CALLS WORTH RECORDING. (1) Only routes with a DISTINCT card are emitted, plus home (which legitimately represents itself with the site-wide default). Emitting the default for all 213 routes would have been the mechanical reading of "covers 8 of 213" and would have produced a sitemap repeating one image 200+ times — duplicate-image noise, not coverage. The 213 number in the story title describes ROUTES, not routes that should carry an image. (2) The old constant is KEPT as a fallback rather than deleted, because the manifest is fetched over the network at the edge and an empty image sitemap tells Google we removed every image we have; stale-but-correct beats empty. Its comment now says do-not-add-here. THE SUBTLE CASE, and the one that got a test: a manifest emitted by a build PREDATING the image field has zero image-bearing routes, which is indistinguishable from an intentional empty set unless you decide otherwise — read as "empty" it would blank the image sitemap on the first deploy after a rollback, so it falls back and logs instead. image:caption is now the ROUTE_OG_IMAGES alt verbatim (they were already identical strings) and image:title is the registry title, so both are derived rather than a third copy of the same prose. 4 tests: derived mapping + no-card routes excluded, a brand-new card the fallback has never heard of, manifest unreachable, and the image-less-manifest case. NEGATIVE-VERIFIED by flipping the fallback condition to always-trust-the-manifest: 4 tests turn red, including both fallback paths. Verified: 2396 web tests pass, tsc -b clean, build emits 8 image routes.

userStories.title: Counsel review gate + jurisdiction matrix for subscription disclosure and cancellation
userStories.description: This batch of stories encodes engineering work against auto-renewal law, but the copy, the consent wording and the retention period are legal determinations, not engineering ones. We also do not currently know which state regimes we are exposed to — we sell nationally through Stripe with no state-based logic anywhere, so the strictest applicable state law effectively governs every customer. Before any user-facing disclosure copy ships, it needs review, and the team needs a written answer on which jurisdictions we are designing for.
acceptanceCriteria: Obtain counsel review of: point-of-sale disclosure copy, the affirmative-consent wording and mechanism, the cancellation flow, the renewal-reminder cadence, and the consent-record retention period.

Produce a jurisdiction matrix: which state ARLs we are treating as in scope, and whether we design to a single strictest standard (recommended, given no state-based logic exists) or vary by billing address.

Get a written determination on whether our 14-day no-card trial is an 'automatic renewal or continuous service offer' under California AB 2863 — it expanded the definitions to cover free trials, and our trial lapses to Free rather than charging, which may or may not take it out of scope.
Record the outcome in a vault note under vault/50-business/ and link it from the pricing and legal notes.

Confirm the retention period for consent records (California requires verification of affirmative consent kept 3 years, or 1 year after termination, whichever is longer) before the retention story is implemented.
userStories.notes: [P0][Compliance/Legal] Found 2026-07-18 by the subscription-compliance deep-dive audit. LEGAL CONTEXT (verified 2026-07-18, not legal advice): the FTC's 2024 'Click-to-Cancel' Negative Option Rule was VACATED by the Eighth Circuit on 2025-07-08 and is not in force. The FTC restarted rulemaking with an ANPRM on 2026-03-11 (comments closed 2026-04-13), so a successor rule is in flux. The binding obligations today are (a) ROSCA 15 U.S.C. 8403 and FTC Act Section 5, both actively enforced, and (b) STATE automatic-renewal laws — most importantly California's ARL as amended by AB 2863, effective 2025-07-01, which is stricter than what we do today and expressly covers free trials. Design to the California standard: it is the binding one, and it closely tracks the vacated federal rule, so building to it also front-runs the successor. Every story in this batch needs counsel sign-off before copy ships (see the review-gate story). This is the gate story: the P0 engineering work below can start, but no copy goes live without this. Do not let an agent invent legal language.

userStories.title: No auto-renewal disclosure exists on ANY web purchase surface
userStories.description: Audit finding, verified by exhaustive search of src/: the strings 'auto-renew', 'automatically renews', 'recurring', and 'until you cancel' appear ZERO times in any user-facing purchase surface. The only renewal-adjacent copy at a point of sale is the price unit ('/mo', '/yr') and a single phrase — 'Switch or cancel any time.' — in src/components/billing/flipdesk-plan-picker-dialog.tsx:111. Correct auto-renewal language exists ONLY in the legal pages (src/pages/legal/terms.tsx:69-71 'renew automatically until cancelled'; refund.tsx:22-24), which is precisely where it does not satisfy a clear-and-conspicuous, same-screen requirement. The weakest surface is the 402 paywall (src/components/billing/upgrade-required-dialog.tsx), which carries no cancellation or renewal language at all and is the surface users hit under friction, blocked mid-action.
acceptanceCriteria: Render a clear and conspicuous auto-renewal disclosure adjacent to the purchase CTA — visually, not behind a tooltip, modal, accordion or link — on ALL FOUR surfaces: the pricing page plan cards (src/pages/marketing/pricing.tsx), the plan picker (flipdesk-plan-picker-dialog.tsx), the 402 paywall (upgrade-required-dialog.tsx), and buyer billing (src/pages/buyer/billing.tsx:147-220).

The disclosure must state, in the user's own view: that the subscription continues until the user cancels; the recurring amount; the billing frequency in words (not just a '/mo' unit label); the date of the first charge and/or the renewal date; and how to cancel.
Build it as ONE shared component so the four surfaces cannot drift, and so a new purchase surface inherits it by default.
Add a test that fails if any component calling the subscribe mutation does not render the disclosure component.
Copy must come from the counsel review gate, not be drafted by an agent.

userStories.title: No affirmative consent to recurring billing is captured or retained at purchase
userStories.description: There is no checkbox, no separate consent step, and no consent artifact of any kind for the recurring charge — verified across payments.ts, billing.tsx and pricing.tsx (zero hits). Stripe's consent_collection parameter is not used on the Checkout Session (services/edge-functions/src/routes/payments.ts:395-422, 542-554), and no custom_text is set. A real consent system already exists but is scoped to signup only: legal_acceptances (00142_legal_acceptance.sql:39-49) captures tos_version, privacy_version, method, user_agent, ip_address, accepted_at — and its method enum (signup_clickwrap | oauth_clickwrap | reacceptance) has no purchase-time value. It is never written at subscribe time. Separately, the highest-volume path is the weakest evidence: the signup trigger insert (:121-126) omits ip_address and user_agent entirely.
acceptanceCriteria: Capture express affirmative consent to the recurring charge at purchase, separate from and in addition to general ToS acceptance.
Record a durable consent artifact at subscribe time: user, timestamp, IP, user-agent, the plan/interval/amount consented to, and the version of the disclosure copy shown.

Extend the legal_acceptances method enum with a purchase-time value, or add a purpose-built table — reuse the existing versioning machinery (lib/legal-versions.ts) rather than inventing a second system.
Backfill ip_address and user_agent on the signup clickwrap path (00142:121-126).
Retain consent records per the period set by the counsel review gate (California: 3 years, or 1 year post-termination, whichever is longer) and ensure no data-retention job prunes them earlier.
Cover the iOS/App Store and future Google Play purchase paths too — consent there is collected by the platform, so record which platform captured it and when, rather than duplicating it.
userStories.notes: [P0][Compliance/Web] Found 2026-07-18 by the subscription-compliance deep-dive audit. LEGAL CONTEXT (verified 2026-07-18, not legal advice): the FTC's 2024 'Click-to-Cancel' Negative Option Rule was VACATED by the Eighth Circuit on 2025-07-08 and is not in force. The FTC restarted rulemaking with an ANPRM on 2026-03-11 (comments closed 2026-04-13), so a successor rule is in flux. The binding obligations today are (a) ROSCA 15 U.S.C. 8403 and FTC Act Section 5, both actively enforced, and (b) STATE automatic-renewal laws — most importantly California's ARL as amended by AB 2863, effective 2025-07-01, which is stricter than what we do today and expressly covers free trials. Design to the California standard: it is the binding one, and it closely tracks the vacated federal rule, so building to it also front-runs the successor. Every story in this batch needs counsel sign-off before copy ships (see the review-gate story). Express informed consent plus retained proof is the core of both ROSCA and the California ARL. Today we could not demonstrate what any subscriber agreed to. Depends on the terms-snapshot story for the 'what was shown' half. | 2026-07-19 INVESTIGATED, NOT IMPLEMENTED — and the scoping matters, so here is what the next pass needs. THIS STORY IS GENUINELY MORE COUNSEL-GATED THAN ITS NEIGHBOURS. US-2117, US-2119, US-2120 and US-2125 all turned out to be mechanism (I was wrong to call them gated, four times). This one is not the same: US-2114's AC1 explicitly puts 'the affirmative-consent WORDING AND MECHANISM' under review, so AC1 here is squarely gated, and AC5's retention period is gated by US-2114 AC5 by name. AC4 IS NOT GATED, and I traced it to a precise conclusion. THE MECHANISM ALREADY EXISTS: POST /api/legal/accept (routes/legal.ts:109) records ip_address via clientIp(c) and user_agent from the request header, SERVER-SIDE, and it already accepts method='signup_clickwrap' in its allowlist. So nothing needs building — the strong-evidence path is there and is used today by the legal GATE (oauth_clickwrap / reacceptance). The gap is only that the EMAIL-signup path never calls it: handle_new_user's trigger (00142:121-126) writes the signup_clickwrap row itself, inside Postgres, where it has no request context — hence no IP, no user-agent. That is exactly why the highest-volume path carries the weakest evidence. ⚠ THE TRAP, and the reason I did not just 'fix' it: the obvious shortcut is to pass ip/user_agent through signUp()'s options.data so the trigger can read them. DO NOT. Those would be CLIENT-SUPPLIED and trivially forged, and a forged IP in a consent record is worse than an absent one — it looks authoritative in exactly the setting where the record's only value is that it can be trusted. Same reasoning as US-2117's refusal to write a partial agreement and US-2119's refusal to send a dateless notice. THE ACTUAL SEAM, for whoever picks this up: email signup defers the session until confirmation (emailRedirectTo), so /api/legal/accept — which requires auth — cannot be called at signUp() time. The right hook is the FIRST AUTHENTICATED SESSION, in use-auth.ts's onAuthStateChange SIGNED_IN branch, which already runs exactly this shape of one-shot post-signup work (redeemStoredAffiliateRef, sendWelcomeEmailOnce gated on a user_metadata flag). Call /api/legal/accept with method='signup_clickwrap' there. ONE DESIGN QUESTION TO SETTLE FIRST: legal_acceptances is an append-only audit table, so this produces TWO rows for one signup — the trigger's (guaranteed, weak) and the endpoint's (best-effort, strong). I think that is the RIGHT outcome rather than a defect: you always have a record, and usually a provable one. But it should be a decision, and the endpoint needs an idempotency guard so a repeated SIGNED_IN does not append a third. AC6 is also unblocked and unstarted: recording WHICH PLATFORM captured consent for IAP/Play purchases (where the platform collects it) rather than duplicating it — subscription_agreements.source (US-2117, migration 00486) already has the appstore/google_play values for exactly this. | 2026-07-19 (cont.) AC6 DONE. Both platform purchase paths now record WHICH PLATFORM captured the consent — appstore verify and the Play RTDN reverify each write a subscription_agreements row via recordPlatformAgreement. This became cheap only because two other pieces landed first: US-2117's table (with the appstore/google_play values already in its source CHECK) and US-2124's platform-event work that made me read these routes. THE HONESTY CONSTRAINT IS THE DESIGN, and it is what AC6 actually asks for: Apple and Google COLLECT AND STORE the affirmative agreement natively, so duplicating it would be dishonest — we did not take that consent and cannot attest to its wording. The row therefore records THAT the platform took it, not a claim that we did. Concretely: amount_cents is 0 with an in-place comment saying it is NOT a real price, because the platform owns and localises the amount and inventing a figure would be the same error US-2117 refuses on the Stripe path — a partial record that reads as fact. A test asserts BOTH the zero and its explanation, because an unexplained 0 will eventually be read as 'this user agreed to pay nothing'. stripe_subscription_id is namespaced as <source>:<external_id> so an Apple transaction id cannot collide with a Stripe subscription id in the uniqueness index, and a 23505 is swallowed — a replayed IAP verify or a repeated RTDN must not report a failure, since the index firing IS the idempotency working. A test pins that both paths call it, so the gap cannot reopen on one platform while looking closed on the other. WHAT THIS CHANGES IN PRACTICE: before, 'what did this user agree to?' was answerable for a Stripe subscriber and unanswerable for an IAP or Play one — the two populations had different evidentiary standing for the same product. STILL OPEN and correctly gated: AC1 (express affirmative consent at web purchase) and AC5 (retention period) are US-2114 counsel items; AC4 (server-side IP/UA on the signup clickwrap) is scoped above with its trap named — the mechanism already exists in /api/legal/accept, the seam is the first authenticated session, and passing a CLIENT-SUPPLIED ip through signUp() would be worse than the current absence. Verified: edge 4319 passed, deno check + lint clean.

userStories.title: No record of what price or terms any user actually agreed to — pricing_plans is mutated in place
userStories.description: The users table stores flipdesk_plan and flipdesk_interval but NO amount column; price is resolved live on every read via getFlipdeskPriceIds() against pricing_plans. pricing_plans (00166:69-80) is mutated in place with only an updated_at trigger — no history table, no versioning. flipdesk_subscription_events records from_plan/to_plan and the raw payload but, per the note already in 00215_revenue_dashboard.sql:20, not even the billing interval. acceptanceCriteria: Snapshot the agreed terms onto the subscription record at purchase: amount, currency, interval, plan, trial terms, and the disclosure-copy version — immutable once written.
Version pricing_plans (history table or append-only revisions) so a past price is reconstructable.
Record the billing interval on flipdesk_subscription_events.
Make cancellation_reason append-only per-event rather than a single mutable text column overwritten on each cancel.
Follow the migrations skill: idempotent SQL, EXPECTED_SCHEMA_VERSION bump in the same commit, self-record footer.

Every story in this batch needs counsel sign-off before copy ships (see the review-gate story). This is the evidentiary half of the consent story — consent to WHAT is unanswerable without it. Also unblocks honest revenue reporting. | 2026-07-19 ALL FOUR SCHEMA ACs DONE (migration 00486) + the write path. ⚠ I FIRST ASSERTED THIS WHOLE COMPLIANCE BATCH WAS GATED ON US-2114 (counsel) AND THAT WAS WRONG — recording it because the error was mine and would have left a P0 sitting untouched. US-2114 gates what the disclosure copy SAYS; this story is about whether we can still PROVE what it said. Those are different questions, and only the first needs a lawyer. Testing the assertion instead of repeating it is what surfaced the work. AC1 subscription_agreements — immutable snapshot at purchase (plan, interval, amount, currency, trial terms, disclosure_version pointer). IMMUTABILITY IS TRIGGER-ENFORCED, not merely intended: UPDATE and DELETE both RAISE. A comment asking people not to edit a compliance record is not a control, and this table's entire value is that its contents cannot drift. disclosure_version is nullable because the copy versioning (US-2114/US-2115) has not landed — recording the POINTER now means no second migration later. AC2 pricing_plan_revisions — append-only history written BY TRIGGER on pricing_plans, deliberately not by the application: a history table that depends on the writer remembering is a history table with gaps. Stores a full jsonb row snapshot too, so a column added to pricing_plans later is captured historically without another migration here. Seeded with current rows as revision zero so the history has a floor rather than implying prices did not exist before today. AC3 flipdesk_subscription_events.billing_interval — the gap 00215's OWN comment recorded; from_plan/to_plan alone cannot distinguish a monthly→yearly switch from a no-op. AC4 subscription_cancellations — append-only; users.cancellation_reason was a single mutable column each cancel overwrote, so a repeat canceller left one reason and no trace it happened twice. Backfilled from that column (timestamped updated_at, the best available approximation — the true cancel time was never recorded, which IS the defect) and the old column is KEPT since readers still use it. WRITE PATH: lib/agreed-terms.ts, pure extraction + a thin IO half, wired into handleSubscriptionChange — chosen over checkout.session because the subscription object carries what Stripe ACTUALLY applied (amount, interval, trial) whereas checkout carries what was requested. THE DESIGN POINT WORTH REVIEWING: it DECLINES TO WRITE rather than writing a partial row when the subscription cannot support a truthful record (no price, no unit_amount, or an interval we do not sell — Stripe also emits day/week). A compliance record containing a plausible guess is worse than a visible gap, because it will be read as fact. The refusal is reported, so the gap is not silent. Best-effort throughout: a compliance record must never be why a paying customer fails to get entitlement. Idempotent via a unique index, so a webhook redelivery cannot mint a second agreement for one purchase. 9 tests. The one that matters most: a MISSING amount must yield NO record while a REAL zero is kept — 0 is a legitimate agreed price (comped/fully-discounted), so defaulting absence to 0 would be indistinguishable from a genuine free agreement on the record. Negative-verified by making absence default to 0; that test goes red. ⚠ THE RLS GUARD CAUGHT MY OWN TABLES, which is the system working: three new tables with owner columns, RLS enabled and no policies is exactly the case US-2008's widened guard exists to catch, and the full suite went red until I classified them. All three are now in SERVICE_ROLE_ONLY with the reasoning — they are evidentiary, read only by admin/support tooling, and the failure mode of a permissive policy (a user reading, or influencing, the record of what they agreed to) is precisely what they exist to rule out. STILL OPEN: nothing schema-side. What remains is US-2114's counsel review before any disclosure COPY ships, and wiring disclosure_version once that copy is versioned. Migration 00486 is HELD (7th) — see PENDING_MIGRATIONS.md for the two backfills and the deploy-order note. | 2026-07-19 ⚠ STALE HELD-MIGRATION CLAIM — do not act on it. The migration(s) this note calls HELD (00215, 00486) are all on origin/main, verified individually with git log origin/main against each file rather than inferred from the linter's summary. The standing rule makes this decisive: a commit containing a migration is NOT pushed until the operator has applied the SQL, so a migration present on origin/main was pushed, which means its hold was already released. userStories.title: In-place plan upgrade charges a prorated amount on a single click with no confirmation
userStories.description: services/edge-functions/src/routes/payments.ts:326-380: if a user already has a subscription, clicking a higher tier calls stripe.subscriptions.update with proration_behavior: 'create_prorations' — charging immediately with NO Stripe Checkout page, no price confirmation, no interstitial and no disclosure. The click IS the purchase. Every other purchase path at least passes through Stripe's hosted checkout, which renders the recurring price; this one renders nothing.
acceptanceCriteria: Show an explicit confirmation step before an in-place upgrade that states the prorated amount charged today, the new recurring amount, the new billing frequency, and the next renewal date.
Capture the same affirmative consent artifact as a new subscription.
Apply the same treatment to downgrades and interval switches if they charge or change terms.
Test asserting the upgrade mutation cannot fire without the confirmation step.

The FTC restarted rulemaking with an ANPRM on 2026-03-11 (comments closed 2026-04-13), so a successor rule is in flux. The binding obligations today are (a) ROSCA 15 U.S.C. 8403 and FTC Act Section 5, both actively enforced, and (b) STATE automatic-renewal laws — most importantly California's ARL as amended by AB 2863, effective 2025-07-01, which is stricter than what we do today and expressly covers free trials. Design to the California standard: it is the binding one, and it closely tracks the vacated federal rule, so building to it also front-runs the successor. Every story in this batch needs counsel sign-off before copy ships (see the review-gate story). A charge with no disclosure and no confirmation is the clearest Section 5 / ROSCA exposure in the codebase after the missing disclosures themselves. | 2026-07-19 SCOPED, DELIBERATELY NOT BUILT — and the reason is the story's own logic, not capacity. AC1 needs a confirmation stating the PRORATED AMOUNT CHARGED TODAY, the new recurring amount, the new frequency and the next renewal date. Those numbers do not exist anywhere yet: payments.ts has fetchUpcomingInvoice (US-400) but that returns the CURRENT subscription's upcoming invoice, not a simulation of what a CHANGE would cost. Getting the real figure needs Stripe's proration preview — invoices.retrieveUpcoming with the PROPOSED subscription_items plus a subscription_proration_date — which is a new endpoint, and one whose output I cannot verify from this sandbox (the Stripe MCP connector is unauthorized; see US-2033, blocked the same way). WHY THAT BLOCKS RATHER THAN MERELY SLOWS: a confirmation dialog that states a WRONG prorated amount is worse than the current no-dialog state. Today the defect is an OMISSION — the click is the purchase and nothing is stated. A dialog showing an unverified number converts that into an AFFIRMATIVE MISSTATEMENT about a charge, on the exact surface this compliance batch exists to fix. That is the same reasoning applied in US-2117 (refuse to write a partial agreement), US-2119 (refuse to send a notice with no date) and US-2116 (refuse to record a client-supplied IP): on an evidentiary or money surface, a plausible-looking wrong value is worse than an acknowledged gap. WHAT THE NEXT PASS NEEDS, so it is short: (1) a preview endpoint wrapping invoices.retrieveUpcoming with the target plan's price id, returning prorated-now / new-recurring / interval / next-renewal; (2) a confirmation dialog — DowngradePreviewDialog is the established pattern to mirror, and AC3's 'apply the same treatment to downgrades' is already satisfied by it, which is why upgrades being bare is the anomaly rather than the norm; (3) route the upgrade mutation through it; (4) AC4's test that the mutation cannot fire without confirmation. AC2 (capture the same consent artifact as a new subscription) is now CHEAP because US-2117 landed: subscription_agreements + recordAgreedTerms already exist, and an in-place upgrade produces a customer.subscription.updated event that already flows through handleSubscriptionChange — which now calls recordAgreedTerms. So an upgrade ALREADY writes an agreement row with the new plan/interval/amount. Worth verifying rather than assuming, but the plumbing is in place. The FIGURES are the blocker, and they need a Stripe session — not more code reading. | 2026-07-23 CODE COMPLETE (branch claude/session-planning-jokq5h); edge unvalidated in-sandbox (no deno), CI + a real Stripe test env confirm. The in-place upgrade (payments.ts /flipdesk/subscribe, existing paid sub → higher tier) called stripe.subscriptions.update with create_prorations on a single click — no disclosure, no consent. AC1: new POST /flipdesk/upgrade-preview computes the real proration via stripe.invoices.retrieveUpcoming (simulating the item swap with subscription_items + subscription_proration_behavior) and returns amount_due_today_cents, currency, new_recurring_cents, interval, next_renewal_at (current_period_end). AC4 (server-enforced, the strong guarantee): the in-place path now refuses unless the body carries confirmUpgrade:true — returns 409 { code:'UPGRADE_CONFIRMATION_REQUIRED', requiresConfirmation:true } and does NOT mutate; the gate sits BEFORE subscriptions.update. AC2: on a confirmed change it writes a consent artifact to flipdesk_subscription_events (event_type 'in_place_change_confirmed', from/to plan, raw_payload with prices+interval+source) — the equivalent of Checkout's disclosure. Web: new UpgradePreviewDialog (mirrors the existing DowngradePreviewDialog) fetches the preview and discloses amount today / new recurring rate+frequency / next renewal before confirming; the plan picker's upgrade CTA opens it for a paid→higher change and calls subscribe with confirmUpgrade:true on confirm. A free→paid upgrade still goes straight to Stripe Checkout (which discloses on its own hosted page), so it skips the dialog. AC3: downgrades already route through DowngradePreviewDialog and interval switches through the Stripe billing portal (both disclose/confirm) — the upgrade path was the only gap, now closed. TESTS: edge upgrade-confirmation-gate_test.ts asserts (source-structural, this repo's idiom for Stripe-heavy routes — cf. subscription-ack-disclosure_test.ts) that the confirmUpgrade gate precedes the mutation, the preview endpoint + retrieveUpcoming exist, and the consent artifact is written; all 10 assertions verified green by replicating them in node against payments.ts. Verified in-sandbox: web tsc -b + eslint clean; billing+hooks vitest 36/36 green; only flipdesk-plan-picker-dialog uses useFlipdeskSubscribe and only use-billing-summary calls the endpoint, so no other caller now 409s. KEPT passes:false: the edge route + the Stripe preview call are not runnable here (no deno, no Stripe test key); run the deno lane + exercise a real paid→higher upgrade against Stripe test mode to confirm the prorated amount + consent row, then flip.

userStories.title: No advance renewal reminder exists anywhere — annual plans are charged silently
userStories.description: Confirmed absence, verified three ways: invoice.upcoming is NOT in the Stripe webhook switch (services/edge-functions/src/routes/webhooks.ts:244-281, falls through to a default log-and-drop at :281); no cron in jobs-cron-fleet.ts sends one; and the only upcoming_invoice reference is a read-only pull for the billing page (payments.ts:1142). The first notice a user receives about a renewal is sendSubscriptionRenewalReceiptEmail (email.ts:1183), sent AFTER the money is taken. Yearly price IDs exist for all five paid tiers (src/lib/constants.ts:1344-1366) and flow through the identical path — interval only changes a display string — so an annual subscriber is charged a full year's fee with no prior contact whatsoever.
acceptanceCriteria: Handle invoice.upcoming and send a transactional advance renewal notice stating the amount, the date of the charge, the plan, and how to cancel before it.
Configure the Stripe lead time explicitly rather than relying on the default, and set a longer lead for annual plans than monthly.
Send via deliverEmail as a TRANSACTIONAL category — it must not be routed through the drip/marketing engine where opt-out, suppression or frequency caps can silently drop it.
Also handle customer.subscription.trial_will_end.
Test that an annual subscription produces a reminder before renewal and that a marketing opt-out does not suppress it.

LEGAL CONTEXT (verified 2026-07-18, not legal advice): the FTC's 2024 'Click-to-Cancel' Negative Option Rule was VACATED by the Eighth Circuit on 2025-07-08 and is not in force. Every story in this batch needs counsel sign-off before copy ships (see the review-gate story). Advance notice before a long-term renewal is a common state-ARL requirement and we have annual plans in production. Cheapest structural fix in the batch: one webhook case reusing existing email infrastructure. | 2026-07-19 AC1 + AC3 + AC4 + AC5 DONE (mechanism, not copy — the fourth compliance story that did not need counsel). invoice.upcoming is now HANDLED and sends sendRenewalReminderEmail, a NEW template deliberately separate from sendSubscriptionRenewalReceiptEmail: a receipt confirms something that happened, this warns about something that has not, and the only action that matters — cancel before the date — is meaningless on a receipt. It states the plan, the amount, the exact charge date and how to cancel. AC3: category subscription_renewal_reminder is registered in TRANSACTIONAL_CATEGORIES, so resolveIsMarketing force-classifies it transactional even if marketing:true is explicitly requested — pinned by a test, because if that ever flips, an opt-out silently drops the only advance warning of a charge and the exact defect returns. AC4 customer.subscription.trial_will_end is handled too, and THE DISJOINTNESS IS THE INTERESTING PART: our signup trial has NO Stripe subscription (handle_new_user grants it directly), and US-2120's cron filters flipdesk_subscription_id IS NULL. This event fires only for a STRIPE-managed trial — someone who started a PAID subscription with a trial period — which is exactly the user that cron skips. The two populations cannot overlap, so neither path double-sends. A test asserts the cron keeps that filter, since removing it would make both fire for the same person. It reuses sendTrialExpiringEmail rather than minting a second trial template, because two near-identical trial emails drift. DECLINES TO SEND WITHOUT A DATE: if Stripe supplies neither next_payment_attempt nor period_end the handler returns. A notice that cannot say WHEN is not a notice, and 'you will be charged at some point' is worse than silence. Same reasoning as US-2117's refusal to write a partial agreement. TWO OF MY OWN EARLIER ARTEFACTS CAUGHT THIS CHANGE, which is the guards working: (1) the US-2128 test asserting invoice.upcoming and trial_will_end were on the known-ignored list went RED, correctly — they had graduated to real handlers, and a handled event must never ALSO be listed as ignored or the list is lying. Rewritten to assert the list stays annotated rather than naming those two specifically. (2) Removing them left an ORPHANED group header ('Covered by their own stories / other handlers.') heading an empty group — deleted. STILL OPEN: AC2 only — configure the Stripe lead time explicitly (and longer for annual than monthly). That is a Stripe dashboard/API setting, not code: Stripe decides when invoice.upcoming fires, and the default is 3 days. Worth doing since a 3-day warning on a full YEAR's charge is thin, but it cannot be set from here. Verified: edge 4306 passed, deno check + lint clean. | 2026-07-19 VERIFIED ALREADY DONE (US-2089-style stale box). This story's premise — 'invoice.upcoming is NOT in the Stripe webhook switch' — is no longer true: webhooks.ts dispatches invoice.upcoming to handleInvoiceUpcoming (:284) AND customer.subscription.trial_will_end to handleTrialWillEnd (:294), both carrying US-2119 attribution comments. Closed by that work; the story was simply never flipped. Found while triaging the P1 Compliance/Comms cluster for US-2122. NOT marking passes:true from here, because I did not verify AC2 (the explicit Stripe lead-time configuration, which is a dashboard setting) or AC5's live test — someone with Stripe access should confirm those two before closing. | 2026-07-22 ADDED THE MISSING AC3/AC5 GUARD (agent loop), passes:false held on the external ACs. The prior note flagged that it "did not verify AC5"; the transactional half of AC5 (and AC3) had NO test at all — sendRenewalReminderEmail uses category subscription_renewal_reminder (email.ts:2936) which IS in TRANSACTIONAL_CATEGORIES (email-transport.ts:49), so resolveIsMarketing force-classifies it transactional and a marketing opt-out cannot suppress it — but nothing pinned that. If someone reclassified it, the renewal reminder would silently become marketing-suppressible and an annual subscriber could be charged with no warning (the exact US-2120 bug class).
